content/docs/(guide)/cli/request-receipt.content:
---
title: Request receipts
description: Inspect the model, provider, usage, cost, latency, and status recorded for local and Cloud requests.
---

A receipt records what served a request. It distinguishes the requested selector from the resolved model and serving provider, so you can inspect [virtual-model resolution](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models) and [Model Fallbacks](/docs/models-routing/model-fallback) outcomes.

[Routing Traces](/docs/routing/routing-traces) explains how to connect request records with routing and attempt spans across a workflow, including correlation and coverage limits.

## Local request receipts

The local metering store records settled requests independently of OpenTelemetry export:

```bash
bro requests --limit 25
```

Each receipt distinguishes the requested selector, resolved model, serving provider, token usage, cost, latency, and status. It remains available when the exporter is disabled and can be inspected with no daemon running.

## Cloud Activity

BitRouter Cloud records request receipts without storing prompt or response bodies. The Activity view shows spend, request count, tokens, model, provider, latency, status, routing profile, and funding source for the active workspace.

The same data is available from the CLI:

```bash
bro cloud usage
bro cloud requests --limit 25
```

Cloud receipts are not span waterfalls. Use your own OTLP backend when you need the complete trace across an agent, router, tools, and every upstream attempt.

## Traces and outcome evidence

Request receipts summarize settled traffic. For an ingress span, routing span, and each upstream attempt, configure [OpenTelemetry in Self-hosting](/docs/self-hosting#opentelemetry). Export and local metering are separate surfaces.

Receipts establish what ran and what it cost. A successful status or a cheaper model does not establish that the task met its objective.

content/docs/(guide)/cli/run-inspect.mdx.content:
---
title: Run & Inspect
description: Operate the local router, preview model routes, inspect settled requests, and automate routine checks.
---

{/* GENERATED by scripts/generate-cli.mjs from cli-overlays/run-inspect.md. Edit the authored input, not this page. */}

Start with a validated [configuration](/docs/routing/configuration). Commands here follow the captured `bro 1.0.0-alpha.33` reference; compare your installed `--help` before using version-specific options.

## Start in the foreground or background

Run the router in the foreground for a terminal session, container, or process supervisor:

```bash
bro serve -c ./bitrouter.yaml
```

Alternatively, start a detached background process:

```bash
bro start -c ./bitrouter.yaml
bro status -c ./bitrouter.yaml
```

The default local listener is `http://127.0.0.1:4356`. `bro status` reports the daemon's state; it does not establish that an upstream model request will succeed. The [Self-hosting guide](/docs/self-hosting) owns service deployment, network exposure, authentication, and telemetry setup.

## Apply configuration changes

Validate the intended file before applying it to the daemon:

```bash
bro config validate -c ./bitrouter.yaml
bro reload -c ./bitrouter.yaml
```

Use the same configuration path to locate the daemon you intend to control. Reload only applies supported changes; consult [reload boundaries](/docs/routing/configuration#apply-and-review-changes) before deciding whether to restart.

```bash
bro restart -c ./bitrouter.yaml
```

Stop the daemon when it is no longer needed:

```bash
bro stop -c ./bitrouter.yaml
```

## Inspect model routes

```bash
bro models -c ./bitrouter.yaml
bro route anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5 -c ./bitrouter.yaml
```

Replace the example selector with one available in your configuration. `bro route` uses the running daemon when reachable and otherwise resolves from the configuration on disk. It is read-only and sends nothing upstream. [Virtual Models](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models#model-selector-forms) explains selector forms; [Auto Router](/docs/routing/auto-router) owns policy initialization and route overrides.

## Inspect settled requests

```bash
bro requests --limit 25 -c ./bitrouter.yaml
```

Inspect the model and provider that served each request, recorded usage, cost, latency, and status. A route preview and a completed request answer different questions. [Request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts) explains the recorded fields; [Routing Traces](/docs/routing/routing-traces) explains correlation and attempt evidence.

Cloud account activity is available through [Cloud Management](/docs/cli/cloud-management#inspect-usage-and-balance).

## Diagnose a failed request

1. Check the daemon with `bro status` and confirm the configuration path.
2. Run `bro config validate` and inspect its warnings as well as its exit status.
3. Use `bro models` and `bro route` to inspect the configured selector and eligible sources.
4. Inspect settled requests with `bro requests`; use the daemon log and configured telemetry for failures not explained by a receipt.

`bro start` writes daemon output to `bitrouter.log` in the configuration directory by default; `--log` selects another path. Foreground `bro serve` writes to its attached process output. For exporter setup and coverage, see [Self-hosting](/docs/self-hosting#opentelemetry).

## Scripting

Use noninteractive onboarding when the required credentials are already supplied through the environment or explicit configuration:

```bash
bro init --yes --use-detected --after exit -c ./bitrouter.yaml
bro config validate -c ./bitrouter.yaml
```

`--yes` does not complete a browser sign-in flow. Use [API-key login](/docs/cli/cloud-management#noninteractive-use) for Cloud automation.

Stop a deployment script when validation fails:

```bash
if ! bro config validate -c ./bitrouter.yaml; then
  exit 1
fi
bro reload -c ./bitrouter.yaml
```

An unset environment reference can be reported as a warning while validation uses a placeholder. Validation is a configuration check, not proof that credentials work or an upstream request will succeed. Inspect the running deployment after applying a change.

Output controls vary by command. The captured local inspection commands describe JSON output, while Cloud commands such as `bro cloud usage` expose their own `--json` option. Consult [Command Reference](/docs/usage/cli) before parsing output; do not infer fields or successful execution from human-readable text alone.

content/docs/(guide)/integration/bro-har.content:
---
title: "bro [harness]"
description: Launch a supported harness with BitRouter routing configured for that process.
---

Use `bro claude` or `bro codex` to open a harness's native interface with its BitRouter connection already configured. BitRouter supplies the gateway endpoint, gateway authentication, and any model override needed for the launch. The harness continues to own its tools, permissions, and session history.

To add BitRouter to an existing native application's model picker instead, use the development [persistent connection guide](/docs/integration/coding-agents#persistent-native-connections). `bro connect` changes the selected native configuration; the launch commands on this page prepare only the child process.

For other supported native harnesses, use the general form `bro launch <harness>`.

<a id="native-launch-and-bro" />

## Native launch boundaries

Native launch keeps you in the harness's interface. It prepares the connection for that process and does not create a BRO Goal or register the process as a managed worker.


The harness retains its private history, compaction, tools, and permission behavior. See the [ACP command reference](/docs/usage/cli#agents-acp-and-mcp) for adapter commands, and [`bro run`](/docs/usage/cli#bro-run) for sending one prompt from a script.

## Start with one command

Once you have a working BitRouter model route and a supported harness installed, run either command from your project:

```bash
bro claude
bro codex
```

To select a route explicitly:

```bash
bro claude --model bitrouter/auto
bro codex --model bitrouter/auto
```

BitRouter prepares the harness's connection and starts its native interface. For a routed local launch, it can start the local daemon if needed. Use [Quickstart](/docs/overview/quickstart) to set up BitRouter and provider credentials first.

## Choose a harness

| Harness | Command | How routing is supplied |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `bro claude` or `bro launch claude` | Child-process environment variables |
| Codex | `bro codex` or `bro launch codex` | Command-line configuration overrides |
| OpenCode | `bro launch opencode` | A generated launch configuration |
| Pi | `bro launch pi` | A generated launch configuration |
| Hermes | `bro launch hermes` | A generated launch configuration |
| OpenClaw | `bro launch openclaw` | A generated launch profile |

The `bro [harness]` short form is available for Claude and Codex; `bro claude-code` is also an alias for `bro claude`. Use `bro launch <harness>` for the other entries above. Native launch support depends on the catalog shipped with your installed version; see the [CLI reference](/docs/usage/cli#bro-launch) for the full command contract.

## What gets configured

For the routed harnesses above, BitRouter prepares the connection for the child process:

- **Endpoint:** the local daemon address derived from BitRouter configuration, or an explicit `--base-url`.
- **Authentication:** `BITROUTER_API_KEY` when set. The local placeholder works only when the daemon allows unauthenticated requests; an authenticated gateway requires a valid BitRouter key.
- **Model:** the daemon-routable id supplied with `--model`, when specified.
- **MCP:** the configured aggregate [MCP gateway](/docs/routing/configuration#agents-and-mcp), when the harness supports injection. Pi does not expose this injection surface.

Claude and Codex receive routing through environment variables or command-line overrides. Harnesses that need generated files receive them under the project's self-ignoring `.bitrouter/launch/` directory. These settings apply to the launched process; BitRouter leaves the harness's normal user configuration in place.

This command prepares the harness to use an existing router configuration. Author providers, credentials, and routes in [bitrouter.yaml](/docs/routing/configuration); look up their field types and defaults in [config reference](/docs/routing/configuration#configuration-reference). A catalog harness using its own authentication, such as `grok` or `agy`, launches directly rather than receiving gateway redirection.

## Select a configuration or endpoint

Point the launcher at a particular BitRouter configuration file:

```bash
bro claude --config ./bitrouter.yaml --model bitrouter/auto
bro launch pi --config ./bitrouter.yaml --model bitrouter/auto
```

Use an explicit gateway endpoint when needed:

```bash
bro codex --base-url http://127.0.0.1:4356 --model bitrouter/auto
```

`--config` selects the BitRouter policy file. BitRouter translates the connection into the selected harness's native configuration format.

## Pass harness arguments

Put BitRouter options before `--`. Everything after it is forwarded to the harness:

```bash
bro claude --model bitrouter/auto -- --permission-mode plan
bro codex --model bitrouter/auto -- --search
```

Permission flags after `--` follow the harness's own rules. See the [ACP command reference](/docs/usage/cli#agents-acp-and-mcp) for commands that connect a client to an adapter.

## Check before launching

Use `--check` to verify the executable, endpoint, and route without opening the harness's interface:

```bash
bro claude --check
bro codex --model bitrouter/auto --check
bro launch pi --check
```

Review the launch report for the route and MCP injection actually applied. `--no-start` prevents automatic daemon startup, and `--no-install` prevents an offer to install a missing supported harness. Passing the launch checks verifies the connection setup; a completed model request provides the next check of the working integration.

<Cards>
  <Card title="Quickstart" href="/docs/overview/quickstart" description="Set up BitRouter and a working model route." />
  <Card title="Configuration (YAML)" href="/docs/routing/configuration" description="Choose the BitRouter policy used by the launcher." />
  <Card title="ACP command reference" href="/docs/usage/cli#agents-acp-and-mcp" description="Inspect ACP adapter and connection commands." />
  <Card title="CLI reference" href="/docs/usage/cli#coding-agents" description="Inspect launch commands and every available option." />
</Cards>

content/docs/(guide)/integration/claude-.content:
---
title: Claude Code
description: Connect Claude Code to local or Cloud BitRouter, configure a Claude-only model pool, and verify the serving route.
---

Keep Claude Code's interface, tools, and permission controls while BitRouter handles its model requests. This guide covers the Claude Code CLI.

## Prerequisites & launch

Install [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup) and [BitRouter](/docs/overview/quickstart). Connect a Claude inference source with [BYOK & Subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions), and confirm that it has a working route. Then run from your project:

```bash
bro claude
```

The launcher configures the child process and can start the local daemon if needed. It leaves your normal Claude Code settings file in place. Without a model override, Claude Code keeps its own model selection. Native launch does not create a BRO Goal; see [the shared launch guide](/docs/integration/bro-harness) for additional options.

## Proxy configuration

Claude Code's [official gateway configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-connect) uses `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and a gateway credential. The examples below use BitRouter's bearer-token authentication. The BitRouter key authenticates the client to the router; upstream provider credentials are configured separately.

### Local

Start the local router with `bro start`, then run these commands in the shell where you launch Claude Code:

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="http://127.0.0.1:4356"
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="${BITROUTER_API_KEY:-bitrouter-local}"
export ANTHROPIC_MODEL="anthropic:claude-sonnet-5"
claude
```

`bitrouter-local` works only when the local router allows unauthenticated requests. If authentication is enabled, export a valid `BITROUTER_API_KEY` first. Use the base URL without `/v1/messages`; Claude Code adds the request path.

### Cloud

Obtain a BitRouter Cloud API key, make it available as `BITROUTER_API_KEY`, and select a Claude route enabled for your Cloud account:

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="https://api.bitrouter.ai"
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="$BITROUTER_API_KEY"
export ANTHROPIC_MODEL="anthropic:claude-sonnet-5"
claude
```

The model ID is an example: confirm account access before using it. A Cloud key does not import your local Claude subscription. Configure [Cloud BYOK](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions#bitrouter-cloud-byok) when bringing an API key; see [pricing](/pricing) for Cloud fees. Self-hosted routing has no BitRouter fee.

Environment changes apply to newly launched processes. Claude Desktop uses a different [third-party inference setup](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-connect#desktop-app).

## Default model pool & customization

Use a Claude-only starting pool. These are explicit example pins, rather than aliases for the newest release or a promise of account availability:

| Claude Code choice | BitRouter model selector | Starting role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sonnet` | `anthropic:claude-sonnet-5` | Default coding model |
| `opus` | `anthropic:claude-opus-4-8` | Complex work |
| `haiku` | `anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5` | Smaller tasks |

Set the mappings before launching Claude Code, using either connection above:

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL="anthropic:claude-sonnet-5"
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL="anthropic:claude-opus-4-8"
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL="anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5"
export ANTHROPIC_MODEL="$ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL"
claude
```

Use `/model` to select a configured choice. The [official model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config) explains alias resolution and model precedence. These mappings select models; they do not install an automatic routing policy or a fallback chain. `bro claude` alone does not install this pool.

To customize it, replace a mapping with another accessible Claude model. Inspect your local sources first:

```bash
bro models --provider anthropic
bro route anthropic:claude-sonnet-5
```

The examples pin the `anthropic` API-key source. A logical ID such as `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5` can instead use eligible connected providers. After separately connecting the `claude-code` subscription provider, set a mapping to `claude-code:claude-sonnet-5` to require that source. Subscription access and limits remain account-dependent. See [subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions#subscriptions) and [model selectors](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models#model-selector-forms).

Keep every mapping in this pool on a Claude model, including any additional family or subagent overrides in your existing settings. For policy-driven selection, configure a Claude-only policy in [Auto Router](/docs/routing/auto-router) before requesting `bitrouter/auto`.

## Verify & troubleshoot

For a local launcher check, run:

```bash
bro claude --model anthropic:claude-sonnet-5 --check
```

Then verify the actual session:

1. Run `/status` in Claude Code and inspect the active model and connection.
2. Ask it to list the files in a small test directory using its tools, then summarize one file in a follow-up turn. Review any permission request normally.
3. For local routing, run `bro requests --limit 10` and match the request time, serving model, and provider. For Cloud, inspect the account's request records. See [Request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts).

A successful reply or launcher check alone does not prove the serving route. Verify streaming, tools, and follow-up turns on the client and source versions you use.

| Symptom | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| Connection refused | Start the local daemon; check the host and port. A remote shell's `127.0.0.1` refers to that remote machine. |
| `401` or an unexpected login prompt | Check that the gateway token reaches the Claude process. Separate gateway authentication from upstream authentication; review conflicting credentials using the [official troubleshooting guide](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-connect#troubleshoot-gateway-errors). |
| Model not found | Check the exact selector, provider activation, account access, and the model mappings. Use `bro route` for the local route. |
| Wrong model after changing settings | Restart Claude Code and inspect `/status`; check `--model`, environment variables, and settings precedence. |
| Tools, thinking, or later turns fail | Check the source's Messages compatibility and beta-field handling against the [gateway compatibility guide](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol). Keep the model fixed while diagnosing the failure. |
| No matching request record | Confirm the session's base URL and the BitRouter instance being inspected; another already-running session may retain its original connection. |

content/docs/(guide)/integration/codex.m.content:
---
title: Codex
description: Connect Codex to local or Cloud BitRouter, configure a GPT-only model pool, and verify the serving route.
---

Keep Codex's interface, tools, and permission controls while BitRouter handles its model requests. This guide starts with the Codex CLI.

## Prerequisites & launch

Install [Codex](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex/cli) and [BitRouter](/docs/overview/quickstart). Connect a GPT inference source with [BYOK & Subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions), and confirm that it has a working route. Then run from your project:

```bash
bro codex
```

The launcher supplies a BitRouter provider through process-specific configuration overrides and can start the local daemon if needed. It leaves `~/.codex/config.toml` in place. Without a model override, Codex keeps its native model selection. Native launch does not create a BRO Goal; see [the shared launch guide](/docs/integration/bro-harness).

## Proxy configuration

Codex's [official gateway configuration](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/enterprise/connect-to-a-gateway) uses a custom provider in the user-level `~/.codex/config.toml` file. On Windows, use `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\config.toml`. Merge the following settings into your existing file; do not duplicate keys or provider tables.

### Local

Start the router with `bro start`. Make a valid gateway key available as `BITROUTER_API_KEY`; only for a local router with authentication disabled, the placeholder can be set with `export BITROUTER_API_KEY=bitrouter-local`.

```toml
model = "gpt-6.1-sol"
model_provider = "bitrouter"

[model_providers.bitrouter]
name = "BitRouter"
base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:4356/v1"
wire_api = "responses"
env_key = "BITROUTER_API_KEY"
http_headers = { "x-bitrouter-harness" = "codex-acp" }
```

Then run `codex`. The `x-bitrouter-harness` header matches BitRouter's native launcher: current BitRouter builds can map declared native GPT names to an active `openai-codex` subscription source. It is a routing hint, not authentication. For an OpenAI API-key source, configure the native-name routes in the next section.

### Cloud

Obtain a BitRouter Cloud API key, expose it as `BITROUTER_API_KEY` to the Codex process, and use the following provider settings instead of the local table:

```toml
model = "gpt-6.1-sol"
model_provider = "bitrouter"

[model_providers.bitrouter]
name = "BitRouter Cloud"
base_url = "https://api.bitrouter.ai/v1"
wire_api = "responses"
env_key = "BITROUTER_API_KEY"
```

Confirm the model selector enabled for your Cloud account and replace the example if needed. A Cloud key does not import a local ChatGPT subscription. For API-key inference, configure [Cloud BYOK](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions#bitrouter-cloud-byok); see [pricing](/pricing) for Cloud fees.

Keep `model` and `model_provider` before the first TOML table. Use a Responses-compatible endpoint and stop the base URL at `/v1`, without `/responses`. Keep the credential itself out of TOML. Restart Codex after changing its configuration; a desktop-launched app also needs access to the credential environment variable.

## Default model pool & customization

Use a GPT-only starting pool, selecting only models available to your account and client:

| Native model ID | Starting role |
| --- | --- |
| `gpt-6.1-sol` | Default coding model in this guide |
| `gpt-6-astra` | Complex work |
| `gpt-6-luna` | Smaller tasks |

These are configuration examples, not a universal account default or an automatically installed routing policy. Codex's [model picker](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/models) determines the available client choices; changing the provider does not grant model access.

For a local OpenAI API-key source, merge these native-name routes into `bitrouter.yaml`. Connect the `openai` provider first, then reload the daemon after saving:

```yaml
models:
  gpt-6.1-sol:
    strategy: priority
    endpoints:
      - provider: openai
        service_id: gpt-6.1-sol
  gpt-6-astra:
    strategy: priority
    endpoints:
      - provider: openai
        service_id: gpt-6-astra
  gpt-6-luna:
    strategy: priority
    endpoints:
      - provider: openai
        service_id: gpt-6-luna
```

These [virtual models](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models) keep the native GPT names while explicitly choosing the upstream source. To require a connected ChatGPT subscription instead, replace `provider: openai` with `provider: openai-codex`. Keep API-key billing separate from subscription access and limits. Cloud routes are configured on the Cloud side, rather than by this local YAML.

Select a pool member with `/model` or for one launch:

```bash
bro codex --model gpt-6.1-sol
```

To customize the pool, add or remove GPT routes and choose the matching model in Codex. Inspect local sources with `bro models --provider openai` or `bro models --provider openai-codex`. Keep custom subagent model settings on GPT models too. For automatic selection, configure a GPT-only policy in [Auto Router](/docs/routing/auto-router).

<Callout type="info">
Codex uses model metadata for context limits, tools, and reasoning settings. A custom alias such as `coding` or `bitrouter/auto` needs a matching catalog entry before you rely on those capabilities. A standard OpenAI model list is not the Codex model catalog. Follow the [official catalog configuration](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/model-catalogs); do not add `model_catalog_url` unless that endpoint actually serves the required format.
</Callout>

## Verify & troubleshoot

Check a local route and launcher without making an inference call:

```bash
bro route gpt-6.1-sol
bro codex --model gpt-6.1-sol --check
```

If you use the subscription's native-name mapping without a virtual model, inspect the explicit route with `bro route openai-codex:gpt-6.1-sol` instead. The generic route command does not carry the harness header.

Then verify the actual session:

1. Run `/status` in Codex and inspect the active provider and model.
2. Ask it to list files in a small test directory using its tools, then summarize one file in a follow-up turn. Review any permission request normally.
3. For local routing, run `bro requests --limit 10` and match the request time, serving model, and provider. For Cloud, inspect the account's request records. See [Request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts).

A successful reply or launcher check alone does not prove the serving route. Check streaming, tools, and follow-up turns with the client and source versions you use.

| Symptom | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| Connection refused or `404` | Check the daemon, host, and `/v1` base URL. Codex needs Responses support; a Chat Completions-only endpoint is insufficient. |
| `401` | Check that `BITROUTER_API_KEY` reaches the Codex process. Separate gateway authentication from upstream provider authentication. |
| Unexpected provider or model | Check `/status`, TOML table placement, and command-line/profile overrides. Restart after changing settings. |
| Model not found | Check account access and the exact local alias or Cloud selector. Confirm the intended API-key or subscription source. |
| Unknown-model warning or incorrect context limits | Check the client catalog and its metadata for the selected model. A working inference route does not establish correct client metadata. |
| Streaming or later tool turns fail | Check Responses event handling and conversation continuity against the [official gateway compatibility guide](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/enterprise/gateway-compatibility). Keep the model fixed while diagnosing the failure. |
| No matching request record | Confirm the process's provider base URL and the BitRouter instance being inspected. |

content/docs/(guide)/integration/coding-.content:
---
title: Coding agents
description: Connect existing agents to BitRouter, choose gateway routes in native model controls, and distinguish persistent setup from launch and ACP.
---

BitRouter separates the **agent harness** that drives the loop from the **model source** that supplies tokens. Connect the agent you already use, then select its BitRouter route in the native model controls. The harness retains its sessions, history, compaction, tools, permissions, and schedules.

## Persistent native connections

<Callout type="info">
`bro connect` is documented here from [BitRouter PR #1016](https://github.com/bitrouter/bitrouter/pull/1016), currently a development CLI capability. Use a build containing that command and check `bro connect --help`. These instructions do not establish availability in an older installed binary or replace the separately captured CLI reference.
</Callout>

`bro connect` configures a persistent native provider. No self-driving extension, separate classifier, or BitRouter-managed agent session is required. After setup, open the native application normally and select the connected route.

```bash
bro connect
```

Choose a client in the menu, review the destination files, and confirm the connection. For a local gateway, prepare working inference sources first with [Quickstart](/docs/overview/quickstart). Setup can start that local gateway after confirmation. It does not install the native client.

| Client | Direct setup | Configuration scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [DeepSeek Harness](/docs/integration/deepseek-harness) | `bro connect deepseek-harness` | Selected initialized profiles in one Harness home |
| [Hermes Agent](/docs/integration/hermes-agent) | `bro connect hermes` | The selected home/current profile, or explicitly named profiles |
| [OpenClaw](/docs/integration/openclaw) | `bro connect openclaw` | One Gateway state root and its agent catalogs |
| [OpenCode](/docs/integration/opencode) | `bro connect opencode` | One native configuration file |
| [Pi](/docs/integration/pi) | `bro connect pi` | One Pi agent directory |

These five adapters add an independent BitRouter provider and retain existing startup defaults. Select BitRouter in the native picker after the required reload. Codex and Claude are also available in the connector menu; their client-specific configuration and restoration differ.

BitRouter is the provider; Automatos is its default router model. The default gateway wire ID is `bitrouter/automatos`. `--model` chooses another exact ID already advertised by the target gateway's `/v1/models`; it does not create a model, strategy, or alias. Display labels and native selection IDs can differ from the wire ID, as described in each client guide.

### Connect an existing gateway

For Cloud or another existing gateway, supply its root URL or `/v1` URL and its gateway credential. For example, after replacing the model placeholder with an exact ID advertised by your Cloud endpoint:

```bash
export BITROUTER_API_KEY='your-bitrouter-gateway-key'
bro connect hermes --base-url https://api.bitrouter.ai \
  --model 'exact-advertised-model-id' --dry-run
bro connect hermes --base-url https://api.bitrouter.ai \
  --model 'exact-advertised-model-id'
```

The explicit endpoint path configures the native client without reading a local BitRouter config or starting a daemon. Remote URLs require HTTPS; HTTP is allowed on loopback. The saved gateway credential is separate from upstream provider keys. For unattended writes, choose an explicit client and add `--yes`.

The default `bitrouter/automatos` must also be advertised before setup succeeds. Availability depends on the chosen gateway configuration and deployment. A callable selector that is absent from `/v1/models` does not pass this connector's catalog check.

### Request context and routing

The connected client sends its normal model request: the selected wire ID, submitted conversation context, and supported tool declarations/results. BitRouter can apply the selected route to that request. The harness determines what is submitted after its own context loading and compaction.

Persistent connection does not export the complete native session store or install a lifecycle observer. It does not itself configure tool permissions, context-profile switching, automatic approvals, or workload learning. Optional self-driving extensions have a separate host-side resource-management role and are not prerequisites for model routing.

### Strategies and workflows

Define model combinations and routing behavior in BitRouter using [Strategies](/docs/routing/strategies) and [Virtual Models](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models). Select a registered gateway route through the harness's own agent, profile, session, or job model settings. The harness remains the owner of those workflow bindings.

For these five independent-provider clients, repeat `--model` to register an ordered collection of exact advertised selectors under one provider. The first retains the existing primary alias/display-name behavior; additional entries use their exact IDs as labels. Duplicate IDs and conflicting native keys are refused. Setup and `--check` validate every ID. Codex and Claude retain their single-model connector contract.

For example, if the gateway advertises both IDs, register them together:

```bash
bro connect hermes --model bitrouter/automatos --model team/background
```

Then choose a registered route in the native workflow settings. Hermes' cron defaults/per-job pins and OpenClaw's per-job model overrides remain harness-owned; `bro connect` does not provide a workflow-binding wizard or rewrite those settings. See the [Hermes](/docs/integration/hermes-agent#chat-and-scheduled-work) and [OpenClaw](/docs/integration/openclaw#agent-and-automation-routes) guides.

A label such as `background` or `flex` does not activate an inference type. The selected gateway must implement the intended policy and support its model/protocol requirements. See [Inference Types](/docs/market/inference-types) for the market capacity types.

### Manage a connection

For these five independent-provider clients, replace `hermes` with the intended client and retain any custom `--instance`:

```bash
bro connect hermes --dry-run
bro connect hermes --status
bro connect hermes --check
bro connect hermes --update
bro connect hermes --remove
```

- `--dry-run` previews files and effects without starting a daemon or writing configuration.
- `--status` checks saved configuration offline. `--check` also verifies the exact gateway model using the saved credential. Neither submits inference or tool calls, and neither proves that a running client has reloaded.
- `--update` replaces the managed provider. Supplying model flags replaces the complete selector list; omitting them preserves it. Supply the full remaining list to drop a selector. Other omitted settings retain the saved connection; an omitted key is reused only for an unchanged endpoint. An update can restore the earlier native startup selection, so reselect BitRouter afterward if desired.
- `--remove` removes owned settings and restores earlier selections only where the connected model is still selected. Later unrelated preferences remain. Saved job/session bindings are not migrated when routes are removed, so change those bindings in the native harness as needed. Edits to owned fields are conflicts to resolve before retrying.

Close config-writing clients during updates or removal. Private connection receipts contain restoration data and credentials; keep them private. For Desktop/Web attached to a different backend, configure that backend on its own host. Each client guide describes reload requirements and state outside the connector's ownership.

After a catalog check, verify inference separately: select BitRouter in the native client, send a small request, exercise any required tool roundtrip, and inspect [request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts). Native default context/cost metadata is not proof of route capacity, actual pricing, or model quality.

## Choose the interface

| Goal | Command | Interface owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add a persistent native provider (development CLI) | `bro connect <client>` | Native client configuration; BitRouter gateway routing |
| Run one turn from a script | `bro run <agent> "..."` | BitRouter, headless |
| Use the harness's own terminal UI | `bro launch <agent>` | The harness |
| Let another ACP client launch the adapter | `bro acp serve <agent>` | The ACP client |

```bash
bro codex
bro run claude "Review the current diff" --format quiet
bro launch opencode
```

`bro connect` changes persistent native configuration. `bro run` and `bro acp serve` use ACP adapters. `bro launch` starts the harness's native interface with process-local routing overrides and leaves normal harness configuration in place. These are separate capabilities; connecting or launching a native client does not create a BRO Goal.

The captured [command reference](/docs/usage/cli#bro-code) documents the released ACP conversation interface. Check native launch and ACP connectivity separately for the adapter and version you use.

## Supported agents

Run `bro agents list` for the catalog shipped by your installed version. Alpha.31 includes local ACP adapters for Claude, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Pi, Hermes, and OpenClaw.

| Friendly id | ACP adapter | Native launch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `claude` | `claude-acp` | `bro claude` or `bro launch claude` |
| `codex` | `codex-acp` | `bro codex` or `bro launch codex` |
| `opencode` | `opencode` | `bro launch opencode` |
| `pi` | `pi-acp` | `bro launch pi` |
| `hermes` | `hermes-acp` | `bro launch hermes` |
| `openclaw` | `openclaw` | `bro launch openclaw` |
| `gemini-cli` | `gemini-cli` | ACP only in the bundled catalog |

Use `bro agents check <agent>` before a long task. It verifies that the adapter can initialize and reports whether its model traffic can be routed through BitRouter.

## What launch changes

See [bro [harness]](/docs/integration/bro-harness) for the shared setup workflow, launch configuration, and command options.

For Claude and Codex, BitRouter passes temporary environment variables or command-line overrides. For OpenCode, Pi, Hermes, and OpenClaw, it writes a generated profile under the working tree's self-ignoring `.bitrouter/launch/` directory and points only the child process at it.

```bash
bro launch pi --model bitrouter/auto
bro launch codex --check
bro launch claude -- --permission-mode plan
```

Arguments after `--` belong to the harness. BitRouter options such as `--model`, `--base-url`, and `--check` must come before it.

Supported native harnesses also receive the aggregate [MCP gateway](/docs/routing/configuration#agents-and-mcp) when they expose a compatible injection mechanism. The launch summary states what was actually routed or injected; Pi and some other harnesses do not expose an MCP injection surface.

## Other harnesses

If a harness is not in the catalog, configure it as a normal API client:

| Protocol | Local base URL | Cloud base URL |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenAI-compatible | `http://127.0.0.1:4356/v1` | `https://api.bitrouter.ai/v1` |
| Anthropic-compatible | `http://127.0.0.1:4356` | `https://api.bitrouter.ai` |

Use a `provider/model` id where the harness accepts a model name. Product-specific configuration keys belong to that harness's documentation; BitRouter only owns the endpoint and routing contract.

## Claude Code

Claude Code owns the agent loop and tools. BitRouter supplies its model route, fallback, policy, and metering.

### Pick a mode

```bash
bro run claude "Summarize this repo"   # headless ACP turn
bro claude                              # Claude Code's native interface
```

`bro launch claude` is the generic spelling of `bro claude`. Both use temporary environment variables for the child process and do not edit Claude Code's user or project settings.

Before launching, verify the executable, daemon, and route:

```bash
bro launch claude --check
```

If the Claude executable is missing, the launcher can offer Claude's official installer. Use `--no-install` when an automated environment should fail instead.

### Select a Claude model

Pin a daemon-routable model before the `--` separator:

```bash
bro claude --model bitrouter/auto
bro launch claude --model anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
```

Arguments after `--` go directly to Claude Code:

```bash
bro launch claude -- --permission-mode plan
```

### Configure Claude Code manually

Use manual environment variables only when Claude Code must start outside `bro launch`. Claude Code appends `/v1/messages`, so the base URL is the host root:

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4356
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=local-placeholder
export ANTHROPIC_MODEL=bitrouter/auto
claude
```

For Cloud, use `https://api.bitrouter.ai` and set `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` to a BitRouter key. An authenticated self-hosted daemon likewise requires a valid BitRouter key instead of the placeholder.

### Use a Claude subscription

Use [BYOK & Subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions#use-a-claude-subscription) for login, explicit subscription routes, and logout. The subscription source is independent of the harness interface.

## Codex

Codex owns the agent loop and tools. BitRouter supplies its model route, fallback, policy, and metering.

### Pick a mode

```bash
bro run codex "Summarize this repo"   # headless ACP turn
bro codex                              # Codex's native interface
```

`bro launch codex` is the generic spelling of `bro codex`. It injects a temporary `bitrouter` model provider into the child process and does not edit `~/.codex/config.toml`.

Verify the executable, daemon, and route before a long run:

```bash
bro launch codex --check
```

### Select a Codex model

Pin a daemon-routable model with BitRouter's option:

```bash
bro codex --model bitrouter/auto
bro launch codex --model openai/gpt-5-codex
```

Arguments after `--` go directly to Codex. Avoid forwarding Codex `-c` or `--config` overrides that replace the injected provider; `bro launch` rejects known conflicting shapes.

### Configure Codex permanently

Use a permanent provider block only when Codex must start outside `bro launch`:

```toml
model_provider = "bitrouter"

[model_providers.bitrouter]
name = "BitRouter"
base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:4356/v1"
wire_api = "responses"
# env_key = "BITROUTER_API_KEY"
```

For Cloud, use `https://api.bitrouter.ai/v1`, set `env_key = "BITROUTER_API_KEY"`, and export a BitRouter key. An authenticated self-hosted daemon requires the same.

<Callout type="warning">
Codex model-provider configuration belongs in the user-level `~/.codex/config.toml`. Project-local Codex configuration does not define model providers.
</Callout>

### Use a Codex subscription

Use [BYOK & Subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions#use-a-codex-subscription) for login, explicit subscription routes, and logout. The subscription source is independent of the harness interface.

## Model sources

A model source is where inference runs and how it is authenticated. BitRouter puts each source behind the same model ids and routing policy, so the calling agent does not need source-specific code.

| Source | Authentication | Setup |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude or Codex subscription | Provider OAuth | `bro providers login <provider>` |
| Built-in BYOK provider | Environment variable or stored key | Export its key or use `bro providers login <provider> --api-key ...` |
| Custom hosted API | API key | Add a `providers:` entry |
| Local inference server | Usually loopback; optional key | Add a `providers:` entry |

Subscription providers do not need a YAML block. Other sources use the same minimal shape:

```yaml
providers:
  my-source:
    api_base: https://example.com/v1
    api_key: ${MY_SOURCE_API_KEY}
    api_protocol:
      - "*": chat_completions
    models:
      - id: example/model
```

Use the upstream's actual served model id in `models`. Keep secrets in environment variables rather than committing them to the file.

### Verify a source

```bash
bro config validate
bro models --provider my-source
bro route my-source:example/model
bro start
```

- `config validate` catches malformed configuration and unsafe upstream URLs.
- `models` confirms the source is in the resolved catalog.
- `route` previews resolution without making an inference request.
- The provider-qualified form pins one source; the bare model id lets BitRouter select among every source that serves it.

To combine sources, define a [virtual model](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models#define-a-virtual-model) or fallback chain. A common pattern is local inference first and a hosted source second.

<Cards>
  <Card title="Local Models" href="/docs/models-routing/local-models" description="Connect Ollama, vLLM, Unsloth, or another OpenAI-compatible server." />
  <Card title="BYOK & Subscriptions" href="/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions" description="Add a hosted API or provider account with a key." />
  <Card title="Run & Inspect" href="/docs/cli/run-inspect" description="Operate the router and inspect routed requests." />
  <Card title="ACP command reference" href="/docs/usage/cli#agents-acp-and-mcp" description="Inspect adapter commands and their options." />
</Cards>

content/docs/(guide)/integration/deepsee.content:
---
title: DeepSeek Harness
description: Add BitRouter to initialized DeepSeek Harness profiles and use its routes from the native model picker.
---

Connect existing DeepSeek Harness profiles to BitRouter. Harness continues to own its Turns, history, tools, and permissions; BitRouter serves model requests through the selected gateway route.

<Callout type="info">
This guide follows the development CLI in [BitRouter PR #1016](https://github.com/bitrouter/bitrouter/pull/1016). Use a build that includes `bro connect`; check `bro connect --help` first. Profiles must already be initialized in the installed Harness.
</Callout>

## Connect your profiles

Install Harness, open the native surface you intend to use to initialize its profile, and prepare a usable [BitRouter gateway](/docs/overview/quickstart):

```bash
bro connect deepseek-harness --dry-run
bro connect deepseek-harness
```

The connector adds an independent **BitRouter** provider through the built-in `llm-pi-ai` adapter and a private stored credential reference. Existing providers and default models are retained. Select the connected model in Harness' native picker; that selection also becomes the profile's default for new sessions.

The default gateway wire ID and model label are `bitrouter/automatos`. `--model` chooses another exact advertised ID; `--display-name` only changes the native label. For Cloud or another existing gateway, use [the shared endpoint and credential setup](/docs/integration/coding-agents#connect-an-existing-gateway).

## Home and profile scope

```bash
bro connect deepseek-harness --instance /path/to/harness-home \
  --profile web --profile headless
```

`--instance` selects the actual Harness home; otherwise discovery uses `DSH_HOME`, then `~/.dsh`. Repeat `--profile` to name initialized profiles explicitly. Without profile flags, a new connection configures the supported initialized profiles detected under that home. It does not initialize missing profiles.

Desktop owns its `desktop` profile and runtime. Open Desktop first to initialize it; configuring an npm CLI installation does not install or configure Desktop's executable. Web, Desktop, and headless compatibility must be checked against their actual profiles.

The connector edits each selected `cordis.patch.yml`, preserves existing provider configuration, and enables the built-in credential service where needed. Unsupported custom bundles or higher-precedence home overrides require explicit configuration. Adapter settings apply on the next request; restart headless processes after changing their startup profile.

To include another initialized profile later, use `--update` with the complete desired profile set. An update without profile flags retains the saved scope.

## Protocol and routing

Chat Completions is the default. `--protocol responses` and `--protocol messages` select the other supported native adapters. One provider uses one protocol; text input is declared, while image and reasoning capabilities are not inferred from a model ID.

Basic routing does not require `dsh-self-driving` or context-profile classification. That separate plugin changes host-side working context between Turns. Repeat `--model` to register several exact advertised IDs in the same provider across the selected profile scope. The first retains the supplied display name; additional labels use exact IDs. Updates replace the full list when model flags are supplied and preserve it otherwise; see [strategies and workflows](/docs/integration/coding-agents#strategies-and-workflows).

## Verify and manage the connection

```bash
bro connect deepseek-harness --status
bro connect deepseek-harness --check
bro connect deepseek-harness --update
bro connect deepseek-harness --remove
```

Use the same custom `--instance` when applicable. `--status` inspects the recorded profile scope offline; `--check` also verifies the gateway catalog with the saved key. Neither sends inference. Select BitRouter, send a small request, test a required tool roundtrip, and inspect [request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts).

Removal covers the complete recorded profile scope and preserves unrelated preferences and providers. Owned settings that were edited, or later profiles referencing the same managed credential, need reconciliation before removal. Credentials and restore receipts are private local files. See [connection management](/docs/integration/coding-agents#manage-a-connection).

content/docs/(guide)/integration/hermes-.content:
---
title: Hermes Agent
description: Add BitRouter to an existing Hermes profile and select its gateway route in the native model picker.
---

Connect an existing Hermes profile to BitRouter. Hermes owns its conversation, memory, tools, approvals, and scheduled jobs; BitRouter receives the model request and applies the selected gateway route.

<Callout type="info">
This guide follows the development CLI in [BitRouter PR #1016](https://github.com/bitrouter/bitrouter/pull/1016). Use a build that includes `bro connect`; check `bro connect --help` before following these steps. The captured CLI reference describes a separate, earlier binary.
</Callout>

## Connect your profile

Install and initialize Hermes, then prepare a usable [BitRouter gateway](/docs/overview/quickstart). Preview the local connection and apply it:

```bash
bro connect hermes --dry-run
bro connect hermes
```

Setup adds a **BitRouter** provider to the selected profile's `config.yaml`. It keeps the current main model, auxiliary models, other providers, and existing jobs. Start or reload that Hermes backend, open its model picker, and choose **BitRouter** and the connected model. No self-driving extension or separate classifier is required.

The default gateway model ID is `bitrouter/automatos`. Hermes picker rows use the exact model ID; the chat chip may shorten it to `automatos`. Changing `--display-name` does not rename Hermes' picker row.

For Cloud or another existing gateway, use [the shared endpoint and credential setup](/docs/integration/coding-agents#connect-an-existing-gateway). `--model` must match an ID advertised by that gateway.

## Choose the right Hermes home

```bash
bro connect hermes --instance /path/to/hermes-home
bro connect hermes --instance /path/to/hermes-root --profile work
```

`--instance` selects an actual Hermes home. Otherwise discovery follows `HERMES_HOME`, or the platform default and Hermes' active profile. Only the selected/current home is configured. Repeat `--profile` to name initialized profiles explicitly; the connector does not create profiles or configure every profile automatically.

CLI, TUI, official Desktop, and Web Dashboard use the configured backend/profile's catalog. If Desktop or Web connects to another machine, run the connector on that backend's host. A long-running backend may need a restart to refresh its catalog; existing chats can retain their own model selection.

## Chat and scheduled work

Select the connected model through Hermes' native model controls. A main-model selection and the auxiliary slots are separate settings.

Hermes also has a cron default (`cron.model` / `cron.model_provider`) and per-job model pins. Those native settings determine which route a job requests. `bro connect` registers the provider; it does not change those settings or assign policies to jobs. See [Hermes model configuration](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/configuring-models) and [scheduled tasks](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/cron).

Repeat `--model` to register separate interactive and background selectors in the same provider, for example `bro connect hermes --model bitrouter/automatos --model team/background` when both IDs are advertised. Automatic discovery stays disabled; the provider contains the explicit model set and uses the first ID as its provider default. Choose chat and cron routes through Hermes itself. Updates replace the full list when model flags are supplied and preserve it otherwise. The shared [strategy and workflow boundary](/docs/integration/coding-agents#strategies-and-workflows) explains the distinction.

## Verify and manage the connection

Use the same `--instance` and profile scope for later operations when applicable:

```bash
bro connect hermes --status
bro connect hermes --check
bro connect hermes --update
bro connect hermes --remove
```

`--status` inspects saved configuration offline. `--check` also checks the gateway catalog with the saved credential; neither submits inference. To verify execution, select BitRouter in Hermes, send a small request, exercise a tool if the workflow needs one, and inspect the gateway's [request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts).

This connector currently supports Chat Completions only. Displayed context limits, prices, and capabilities for an unknown model are Hermes defaults, not verified gateway metadata.

Credentials are persisted in the private profile configuration and BitRouter connection receipt. Removal restores the earlier main route if any connected model is still selected, while retaining unrelated preferences and auxiliary settings. Desktop can retain a manual composer pin after removal; reopen its picker and choose another available model. Resolve edits to the managed provider before updating or removing it. See [connection management](/docs/integration/coding-agents#manage-a-connection).

content/docs/(guide)/integration/opencla.content:
---
title: OpenClaw
description: Add BitRouter to an existing OpenClaw gateway and select its route from native agent and automation model controls.
---

Connect the OpenClaw gateway you already use to BitRouter. OpenClaw retains its agents, sessions, memory, tools, and automations; the gateway model selector determines which BitRouter route receives each model request.

<Callout type="info">
This guide follows the development CLI in [BitRouter PR #1016](https://github.com/bitrouter/bitrouter/pull/1016), validated with OpenClaw 2026.10.9. Use a build with `bro connect` and check `bro connect --help` first. Older OpenClaw configurations using `agents.list` require an upgrade.
</Callout>

## Connect your gateway

Install and initialize OpenClaw, then prepare a usable [BitRouter gateway](/docs/overview/quickstart):

```bash
bro connect openclaw --dry-run
bro connect openclaw
```

Setup adds an independent BitRouter provider to one OpenClaw state root and keeps existing agent defaults, providers, and fallback selections. Start or reload that native gateway yourself. Its TUI, Web Control UI, and connected Desktop companion use the same backend catalog. No routing plugin is required.

In the TUI, select:

```text
/model bitrouter/automatos
```

In the native model picker, the provider group is currently **Bitrouter**, with **automatos** beneath it. The native alias resolves to the exact gateway request ID `bitrouter/automatos`.

For Cloud or another existing gateway, use [the shared endpoint and credential setup](/docs/integration/coding-agents#connect-an-existing-gateway). `--model` selects an exact advertised wire ID; `--display-name` only changes its label.

## Select the state root

```bash
bro connect openclaw --instance /path/to/openclaw-state
```

`--instance` accepts the state directory or a config file inside it. Default discovery follows `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`, then `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, then the normal OpenClaw home. Start OpenClaw with the matching state/config settings. A config-path override alone does not relocate native agent state.

The connection applies to configured agents and their model catalogs in that gateway instance. Existing model policies must allow the connected route; setup does not widen those policies. Select a different native OpenClaw profile through its actual state directory, not BitRouter's `--profile` flag.

A Desktop or Web client attached to a remote gateway needs configuration on that gateway's host. Local file changes do not configure a remote server. Existing sessions can retain their selected models.

## Agent and automation routes

Use OpenClaw's native agent/session model controls and per-job automation overrides to select a registered route. The connector does not change schedules, job inference accounts, or model bindings. See [agent models](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/config-agents/models) and [automation model selection](https://docs.openclaw.ai/automation/cron-jobs/payloads).

Repeat `--model` to register multiple advertised selectors. The first keeps the `automatos` alias; additional entries use exact-ID labels. Native picker refs are `bitrouter/<wire-ID>`, without repeating the prefix when the wire ID already starts with `bitrouter/`. Additional refs that collide with the primary alias, or IDs with overlapping native refs, are refused. Existing model policies must permit every added route; allowing the primary alias does not authorize other models. Checks and selection restoration recognize OpenClaw's canonical refs. `--update` replaces the complete list when model flags are supplied, and preserves it otherwise. Workflow bindings stay in OpenClaw; saved jobs are not migrated when selectors are removed. See the shared [strategy and workflow boundary](/docs/integration/coding-agents#strategies-and-workflows).

## Verify and manage the connection

Use the same `--instance` for a nondefault connection:

```bash
bro connect openclaw --status
bro connect openclaw --check
bro connect openclaw --update
bro connect openclaw --remove
```

`--status` is an offline configuration check. `--check` also verifies catalog access with the saved credential; neither runs inference. Select BitRouter in the native client, send a small request, test any required tool roundtrip, and inspect [request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts) to verify actual execution.

The connector supports Chat Completions only. Native streaming and file-read tool turns were exercised with a deterministic upstream; this does not establish real-model quality or compatibility with arbitrary upstreams. OpenClaw's displayed default limits and cost estimates are not verified Automatos metadata.

## Credentials and removal

The gateway key is stored in a private file beside the selected config and referenced through OpenClaw's native file SecretRef. Config backups and generated model catalogs receive references rather than the literal key. JSON5 comments and unrelated configuration are preserved. Configurations using `$include` need explicit consolidation before this adapter can manage them.

Stop the selected native gateway before removal so it releases its in-memory credential. Removal restores owned defaults still selecting the connected model and removes the managed provider, alias, credential source, and recorded catalog replicas. Existing sessions must choose another available model afterward. Later references to the managed secret or unrecorded provider replicas need reconciliation before removal. See [connection management](/docs/integration/coding-agents#manage-a-connection).

content/docs/(guide)/integration/opencod.content:
---
title: OpenCode
description: Add a persistent BitRouter provider to OpenCode while retaining its native sessions, tools, and interface.
---

Connect OpenCode's existing backend to BitRouter. OpenCode keeps its session history, compaction, tool loop, and permissions. BitRouter receives the submitted model request and serves the selected route.

<Callout type="info">
This guide follows the development CLI in [BitRouter PR #1016](https://github.com/bitrouter/bitrouter/pull/1016). Use a build that includes `bro connect`; check `bro connect --help` first. The captured CLI reference describes a separate, earlier binary.
</Callout>

## Connect OpenCode

Install OpenCode and prepare a usable [BitRouter gateway](/docs/overview/quickstart):

```bash
bro connect opencode --dry-run
bro connect opencode
```

Setup adds `provider.bitrouter` to the selected OpenCode configuration. Existing providers, the main `model`, and `small_model` remain unchanged. Restart OpenCode CLI/TUI or its local Desktop/Web server, then choose **BitRouter** and the connected model (`/models` in the TUI).

The native selection ID is `bitrouter/automatos`. Its underlying gateway model defaults to the same string. `--model` changes the exact gateway wire ID while retaining that native selection key; `--display-name` changes the label. Labels do not create routes.

For Cloud or another existing gateway, use [the shared endpoint and credential setup](/docs/integration/coding-agents#connect-an-existing-gateway).

## Configuration and protocol

```bash
bro connect opencode --instance /path/to/opencode.jsonc
```

`--instance` accepts a config file or directory. Without it, discovery follows `OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR`, `OPENCODE_CONFIG`, then the normal global config directory. The connector preserves JSONC comments and unrelated settings. It does not implicitly write a project configuration. Project, inline, or managed settings can still take precedence.

| Connector protocol | OpenCode provider SDK | Gateway API |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `chat-completions` (default) | `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` | `/v1/chat/completions` |
| `responses` | `@ai-sdk/openai` | `/v1/responses` |
| `messages` | `@ai-sdk/anthropic` | `/v1/messages` |

A Desktop/Web client connected to a remote OpenCode server needs configuration on that server. Changing local files does not update a remote backend. Restart the backend that reads the selected config when its catalog is stale.

No `opencode-self-driving` plugin, classification model, or host-side model pool is required for this connection. That separate experiment controls additional host-side resource selection. Repeat `--model` to register additional advertised routes. The first retains the native `bitrouter/automatos` key; each additional entry uses `bitrouter/<wire-ID>`. An additional ID equal to `automatos` conflicts with that primary key and is refused. Updates replace the full list when model flags are supplied and preserve it otherwise; see [strategies and workflows](/docs/integration/coding-agents#strategies-and-workflows).

## Verify and manage the connection

```bash
bro connect opencode --status
bro connect opencode --check
bro connect opencode --update
bro connect opencode --remove
```

Use the same `--instance` for a custom config. `--status` checks saved configuration offline. `--check` also checks the exact advertised model using the saved gateway credential; it does not send inference. Select BitRouter in OpenCode, send a small request, exercise a required tool roundtrip, and inspect [request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts).

No model context limit, price, modality, or reasoning capability is inferred from an ID. Validate those requirements against the chosen gateway route and OpenCode version.

The key is stored in the private owned provider configuration and connection receipt. Updates replace the managed connection; saved defaults selecting BitRouter can return to their earlier native values. Removal restores owned selections when applicable and preserves unrelated later changes. Edited managed provider fields are conflicts. See [connection management](/docs/integration/coding-agents#manage-a-connection).

content/docs/(guide)/integration/pi.mdx.content:
---
title: Pi
description: Configure a persistent BitRouter provider in Pi and route native CLI or TUI requests through the gateway.
---

Add BitRouter to Pi's native model picker. Pi owns generation, history, compaction, tools, and permissions; BitRouter serves requests using the selected gateway route.

<Callout type="info">
This guide follows the development CLI in [BitRouter PR #1016](https://github.com/bitrouter/bitrouter/pull/1016). Use a build that includes `bro connect`; check `bro connect --help` first. The connector targets current `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` configuration; legacy `@mariozechner/pi-coding-agent` credential behavior is not covered by this guide.
</Callout>

## Connect Pi

Install Pi and prepare a usable [BitRouter gateway](/docs/overview/quickstart):

```bash
bro connect pi --dry-run
bro connect pi
```

The command adds a `bitrouter` provider to `models.json` and a saved credential to `auth.json` in Pi's agent directory. Existing providers, credentials, and startup defaults are retained. Open `/model` to reload the configuration, then select the connected model under **bitrouter**.

The default wire ID is `bitrouter/automatos`. Pi picker rows show exact model IDs; `--display-name` supplies detail/search text. Pi's fully qualified local identity includes the provider plus the wire ID, so a repeated provider segment there does not change the request model.

For Cloud or another existing gateway, use [the shared endpoint and credential setup](/docs/integration/coding-agents#connect-an-existing-gateway). Repeat `--model` to register several exact advertised IDs in the same provider. `--display-name` applies to the first entry; additional labels use exact IDs. Updates replace the full list when model flags are supplied and preserve it otherwise. Removal recognizes startup selections of any registered model.

## Agent directory and protocol

```bash
bro connect pi --instance /path/to/pi-agent-dir
```

The agent directory is selected by `--instance`, then `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR`, then `~/.pi/agent`. Supply the agent directory itself. SDK clients using another `agentDir` need that same directory configured explicitly.

Chat Completions is the default protocol. `--protocol responses` uses Responses; `--protocol messages` uses Anthropic Messages. Choose a protocol supported by the actual route. Configuration does not certify upstream tool or media compatibility.

The connector does not require `pi-self-driving`, a classification model, or a five-tier model pool. That separate extension manages host-side resource selection; the basic gateway connection works independently. See [strategies and workflows](/docs/integration/coding-agents#strategies-and-workflows) for registering multiple selectors and native workflow ownership.

## Verify and manage the connection

```bash
bro connect pi --status
bro connect pi --check
bro connect pi --update
bro connect pi --remove
```

Use the same `--instance` for a custom agent directory. `--status` checks saved configuration offline; `--check` also verifies the exact model in the gateway catalog using the saved key. Neither sends inference. Select BitRouter, send a small request, exercise the tools your workflow uses, and inspect [request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts).

Pi supplies defaults for omitted model metadata. Displayed context windows or zero estimated cost do not establish the gateway route's actual limits or pricing.

Updating replaces the managed connection and can restore its saved native startup default; select BitRouter again afterward if desired. Removal preserves unrelated provider/auth/preferences and restores the previous default only while the connected model is still selected. Resolve edits to managed provider or credential fields before changing the connection. See [connection management](/docs/integration/coding-agents#manage-a-connection).

content/docs/(guide)/market/buy-inferenc.content:
---
title: Buy Inference
description: Access inference through BitRouter for your applications and coding agents.
---

For the routing concept behind cache-aware source selection, see [State Affinity](/docs/routing/state-affinity).

Elastic Inference charges the supplier’s actual settled inference cost plus the Cloud platform fee: **$0.01 per million processed input + output tokens — early access pricing**. The platform fee is counted once per request, including when using Cloud Auto Routing. The buyer’s total price cap includes both charges, calculated using the full output limit for budget checks. See [Price-Time Priority](/docs/market/price-time-priority#cloud-platform-fee).

content/docs/(guide)/market/inference-ti.content:
---
title: Inference Tiers
description: Compare the evidence and security requirements for Unverified, Verified, and Secured inference.
---

Inference tiers describe the evidence and security requirements for a result. [Inference Types](/docs/market/inference-types) describes how capacity is made available. These tier definitions are a market design preview.

## Unverified

The source returns a result without independent evidence of which model ran or how the response was produced. This can describe sources outside the BitRouter platform, such as arbitrary endpoints connected to the OSS router.

## Verified

Evidence connects the request and response to execution against the declared model version, weights, and precision. See [what the BitRouter platform verifies](/enterprise#verification) for the verification scope.

## Secured

The proposed tier adds specified security requirements for execution and data handling to the verification evidence. The applicable safeguards depend on the service terms.

content/docs/(guide)/market/inference-ty.content:
---
title: Inference Types
description: Compare on-demand, interruptible, and reserved inference capacity.
---

An inference type describes how capacity is made available and whether the supplier can interrupt execution. These types describe the market design. For verification and security requirements, see [Inference Tiers](/docs/market/inference-tiers).

## On-demand

Use capacity available when the request is accepted. On-demand inference suits interactive work and other requests that need a prompt start.

## Interruptible

Use capacity that the supplier can reclaim while inference is running. Interruptible inference suits workloads that can tolerate an interrupted attempt, such as background jobs that can be run again.

## Reserved

**Coming soon.** Arrange capacity ahead of time for scheduled or recurring workloads. See the [Enterprise capacity reservations alpha](/enterprise#enterprise-reservation-title) for the existing alpha test.

content/docs/(guide)/market/price-time-p.content:
---
title: Price-Time Priority
description: How price and time shape an inference purchase, including supplier charges and Cloud platform fees.
---

## Price and time

A buy order sets a maximum total charge and a window for accepting an offer. Within those limits, the order design lets buyers prefer a lower estimated charge or an earlier estimated completion. The purchase window controls when an offer can be accepted. Completion timing follows the accepted offer's service terms. See the [illustrative buy limit orders](/docs/overview/elastic-inference#buy-limit-orders).

## Cloud platform fee

Cloud Auto Routing and Elastic Inference share **$0.01 per million processed input + output tokens — Early access pricing**. Processed tokens are verifiable actual input + output tokens processed by Cloud, accumulated across requests. A request is counted once, including when Auto Routing selects Elastic Inference.

Provider or supplier inference charges are separate. Elastic Inference adds the Cloud platform fee to the supplier's actual settled inference charge, with no percentage-based transaction fee. Buyer price caps include both charges: estimates use expected output, budget checks use the full output limit, and final platform fees use actual processed input + output tokens.

## Welcome credit

**First billion tokens on us. No credit card required.**

New Cloud accounts receive a one-time **$10 welcome credit toward platform fees only**, equivalent to one billion processed input + output tokens at the current early access rate. Provider inference charges still apply.

## Other options and charges

OSS self-hosting is free of BitRouter fees; provider and infrastructure costs remain separate. Enterprise pricing is custom. Payment-processing charges are a separate category.

See [platform pricing](/pricing) for the public pricing options, [Buy Inference](/docs/market/buy-inference) for the buyer guide, and [Sell Inference](/docs/market/sell-inference) for the supplier guide.
