The platform fee is counted once per request, including when using Cloud Auto Routing. See [Price-Time Priority](/docs/market/price-time-priority#cloud-platform-fee).

content/docs/(guide)/models-routing/byok.content:
---
title: BYOK & Subscriptions
description: Connect API keys, subscription logins, multiple accounts, and custom endpoints to BitRouter.
---

A **provider** tells BitRouter where and how to call an upstream. A **model** is a routable id declared by one or more providers. Bring an API key, sign in to a supported subscription provider, or configure a custom endpoint to make its models available to your deployment. A provider account and an agent harness are separate choices.

## Choose the path

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| A supported provider with your API key | Environment variable or an empty built-in provider block |
| Claude or Codex subscription | [Subscription login](#subscriptions) |
| Local inference | [Local Models](/docs/models-routing/local-models) |
| A private or OpenAI-compatible endpoint | A custom `providers` entry below |
| A provider everyone should discover | A pull request to the open registry |
| Your provider key on BitRouter Cloud | Cloud BYOK |

## Built-in providers with your own key

The local binary detects common provider credentials without a config file:

```bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
export GEMINI_API_KEY=...

bro providers list
bro start
```

To make the enabled set explicit, add empty provider blocks and let them inherit the bundled registry definition:

```yaml
providers:
  openai: {}
  anthropic: {}
  google: {}
```

Keep credentials in environment variables. Run `bro reload` after rotating a key and `bro providers list` to confirm which sources are active.

## Subscriptions

Subscription credentials are separate from API keys and from the harness you launch. A configured subscription source requires an explicit provider-qualified route; bare model selection does not silently consume a personal subscription. Available models and protocols depend on the selected source.

### Use a Claude subscription

The `claude-code` provider uses a Claude Pro or Max credential instead of an Anthropic API key. It is separate from the standard `anthropic` provider, but it can be used with [the Claude Code harness](/docs/integration/claude-code).

Sign in:

```bash
bro providers login claude-code
```

BitRouter adopts a compatible local Claude Code login when possible and otherwise starts the provider's login flow. The stored credential refreshes automatically; no `providers:` block is required.

Verify the models and route:

```bash
bro models --provider claude-code
bro route claude-code:claude-sonnet-4-6
```

Use the provider-qualified id to require the subscription source. A request routed to `anthropic:<model>` uses `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` instead.

Then launch any Claude Code mode normally:

```bash
bro start
bro claude
# or: bro run claude "Summarize this repo"
```

Sign out with:

```bash
bro providers logout claude-code
```

This removes BitRouter's stored subscription credential and route. It does not modify Claude Code's own configuration.

<Callout type="info">
Provider login and BitRouter Cloud login are separate. `bro providers login claude-code` authenticates the upstream subscription; `bro cloud login` authenticates your BitRouter account.
</Callout>

### Use a Codex subscription

The `openai-codex` provider uses a ChatGPT Plus or Pro credential and the Codex Responses backend. It is separate from the standard `openai` API-key provider, but it can be used with [the Codex harness](/docs/integration/codex).

Sign in:

```bash
bro providers login openai-codex
```

BitRouter can import a compatible local Codex login or start the provider's browser flow. For automation that must not open a browser:

```bash
bro providers login openai-codex --import-existing --no-browser
```

No `providers:` block is required. Verify the models and route:

```bash
bro models --provider openai-codex
bro route openai-codex:gpt-5-codex
```

Use the provider-qualified id to require the subscription source. A request routed to `openai:<model>` uses `OPENAI_API_KEY` and the public OpenAI API instead.

Then launch any Codex mode normally:

```bash
bro start
bro codex
# or: bro run codex "Summarize this repo"
```

Sign out with:

```bash
bro providers logout openai-codex
```

This removes BitRouter's stored subscription credential. It does not sign the Codex CLI out of its own account.

<Callout type="info">
Provider login and BitRouter Cloud login are separate. `bro providers login openai-codex` authenticates the upstream subscription; `bro cloud login` authenticates your BitRouter account.
</Callout>

## Custom endpoints and models

Any endpoint using a supported outbound protocol can become a provider:

```yaml
providers:
  my-cluster:
    api_base: "https://llm.internal.example/v1"
    api_key: "${MY_CLUSTER_TOKEN}"
    api_protocol:
      - "*": chat_completions
    models:
      - id: team/llama-3.1-8b
        capabilities: [tools, structured_outputs]
```

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `api_base` | Upstream base URL |
| `api_key` | Optional credential; use an environment reference |
| `api_protocol` | Model-pattern to ordered protocol mapping |
| `models[].id` | Canonical model id the provider declares |
| `models[].capabilities` | Positively verified features used during route filtering |
| `priority` / `tags` | Deterministic ordering and routing filters |

Supported built-in protocol names are `chat_completions`, `responses`, `messages`, and `generate_content`. A model-specific `api_protocol` overrides the provider pattern.

Do not advertise a capability merely because the protocol can encode it. Declare only behavior verified for that exact provider/model route.

### Validate and route

```bash
bro config validate -c bitrouter.yaml
bro models --provider my-cluster
bro route my-cluster:team/llama-3.1-8b -c bitrouter.yaml
```

The `provider:model` selector pins one provider. The bare model id joins every active provider that declares that id; use [Virtual Models](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models) to define a named route and [Model Fallbacks](/docs/models-routing/model-fallback) for replacement behavior.

For Ollama, vLLM, Unsloth, and similar servers, use the shorter [Local Models](/docs/models-routing/local-models) recipe.

## Multiple accounts

One provider can expose several credentials:

```yaml
providers:
  openai:
    account_strategy: failover
    accounts:
      - label: primary
        api_key: "${OPENAI_KEY_PRIMARY}"
      - label: backup
        api_key: "${OPENAI_KEY_BACKUP}"
```

`failover` preserves declared order and advances after retryable or credit-exhaustion failures. `balance` rotates the first account, while the remaining accounts still form the request's fallback chain.

## BitRouter Cloud BYOK

Cloud BYOK stores a provider credential for your account and routes eligible calls through it. The recommended path is the Cloud console, which fetches the node's encryption public key and seals the provider key in the browser before upload.

Cloud Auto Routing with BYOK uses **$0.01 per million processed tokens — early access pricing**, based on verifiable actual input + output tokens processed by BitRouter Cloud. The same platform fee applies to Elastic Inference and is counted once per request, including when routing into the market. Your provider bills model inference separately under its own rates. Local, self-hosted BYOK routing has no BitRouter fee. See [pricing](/pricing).

For automated onboarding, start with the [BYOK API reference](/docs/reference/byok/getEncryptionPubkey). Keep encryption and upload code in the client; never send a plaintext provider key to a logging or application endpoint.

## Contribute a provider

Private config affects only your deployment. To make a provider discoverable to every BitRouter installation, add its manifest to the [open provider registry](https://github.com/bitrouter/bitrouter/tree/main/registry) and submit a pull request. Registry data can describe endpoints, protocols, models, capabilities, pricing, and authentication conventions; provider-specific executors or OAuth flows still require code.

  <Card title="Configuration (YAML)" href="/docs/routing/configuration" description="Validate and apply the complete desired-state contract." />
</Cards>

content/docs/(guide)/models-routing/loca.content:
---
title: Local Models
description: Connect Ollama, vLLM, Unsloth, or another OpenAI-compatible model server to BitRouter.
---

Local inference servers share one BitRouter integration: expose an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, add it under `providers`, and declare the model ids that endpoint serves.

## Common servers

| Server | Typical API base | Authentication | Model id source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ollama | `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1` | None on loopback | `ollama list` |
| vLLM | `http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1` | Optional `--api-key` | Served model name |
| Unsloth | `http://127.0.0.1:8888/v1` | Server-issued key | `GET /v1/models` |

Ports and authentication can be changed by the server. Treat the table as a starting point and confirm the endpoint locally.

## Configure BitRouter

```yaml
providers:
  local:
    api_base: http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1
    api_protocol:
      - "*": chat_completions
    models:
      - id: llama3.1
```

For an authenticated server, add an environment-backed key:

```yaml
providers:
  local:
    api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1
    api_key: ${LOCAL_INFERENCE_API_KEY}
    api_protocol:
      - "*": chat_completions
    models:
      - id: my-served-model
```

The model id must match what the server accepts. For vLLM, that may be the full model repository id or the value supplied with `--served-model-name`. For Ollama, it is the pulled model tag. For Unsloth, use the id returned by its models endpoint.

## Verify and route

```bash
bro config validate
bro models --provider local
bro route local:llama3.1
bro start
```

The provider-qualified id pins the local server. A bare model id lets BitRouter use another configured source serving the same model, which is useful for local-first fallback.

<Callout type="warning">
Keep an unauthenticated inference server on loopback or a trusted private network. Binding it publicly without its own authentication exposes model capacity outside BitRouter's policy boundary.
</Callout>

## Server-specific references

- [Ollama OpenAI compatibility](https://docs.ollama.com/api/openai-compatibility)
- [vLLM OpenAI-compatible server](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/serving/openai_compatible_server/)
- [Unsloth API endpoint](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/api)

<Cards>
  <Card title="Bring your own model" href="/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions#custom-endpoints-and-models" description="Understand the general contract for any model you serve." />
  <Card title="Model Fallbacks" href="/docs/models-routing/model-fallback#fallback-chains" description="Fall back from local inference to a hosted source." />
  <Card title="Configuration (YAML)" href="/docs/routing/configuration" description="Place the provider block in the complete desired-state contract." />
</Cards>

content/docs/(guide)/models-routing/mode.content:
---
title: Model Fallbacks
description: Define replacement routes and understand when a failed inference request advances to another provider or model.
---

Fallback tries another eligible endpoint after a retryable inference failure. A [virtual model](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models) gives configured endpoints one callable name; fallback determines how a failed attempt is replaced.

Selecting a cheaper model for a normal call is a routing decision. An HTTP success does not trigger fallback merely because the answer is poor; task quality requires a separate evaluation.

## Same-model provider fallback

A logical model id can be served by more than one connected provider. Request the logical id to keep eligible provider alternatives available:

```text
openai/gpt-5.4
```

BitRouter applies provider filters, capability and protocol requirements, then orders eligible providers by configured or registry priority and provider id. A retryable failure can advance through that chain.

A provider-qualified selector pins one provider:

```text
openai:openai/gpt-5.4
```

That selector does not automatically expand into other providers or a different model. A configured provider can still have its own account fallback.

## Fallback chains

Use a [virtual model](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models#define-a-virtual-model) to expose an ordered chain behind one name. The `coding` example in that guide declares an OpenAI endpoint followed by an Anthropic endpoint with `strategy: priority`.

A request for `coding` tries its eligible endpoints in YAML order. Connect and validate both sources first using [BYOK & Subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions). Adding another model to the available catalog does not automatically make it a replacement for the first.

Use `strategy: cascade` only when the endpoints are interchangeable and selection preferences may reorder or filter them. The self-hosted alpha.33 `cost` and `latency` sorts use deterministic priority/provider-id ordering rather than measured live optimization.

## Which failures advance the chain?

| Failure | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Upstream `5xx` | Retryable; another endpoint may serve the request |
| `408`, `429`, transport failure, or timeout | Retryable |
| Invalid upstream response or exhausted provider credit | Retryable |
| Other upstream client-side `4xx` | Fail immediately rather than advancing |
| Successful response with an unsatisfactory answer | Does not establish a retryable transport failure |

Fallback remains subject to the request's capabilities, protocol, access policy, and execution limits. It cannot make an incompatible model eligible or guarantee that any replacement succeeds.

## Account fallback

Multiple credentials for one provider are a separate level of replacement:

Use `account_strategy: failover` to preserve declared account order, or `balance` to rotate the first account while retaining the remaining fallback chain. Configure credentials in [BYOK & Subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions#multiple-accounts).

These settings change credential selection; they do not substitute a different model.

## Local-first fallback

A local server can participate like any other provider. Connect it with [Local Models](/docs/models-routing/local-models), then include its served model in an explicit priority chain before a hosted replacement.

Keep the selector distinction clear: `local:llama3.1` pins the local provider, while a virtual model can name a local endpoint followed by a different hosted model. The models in that chain must support the request's required features.

## Verify the chain and the serving route

```bash
bro config validate -c bitrouter.yaml
bro route coding -c bitrouter.yaml
bro requests --limit 25
```

`bro route` previews the candidate chain without making an inference request. A settled [request receipt](/docs/cli/request-receipts) identifies the actual serving model and provider. [OpenTelemetry](/docs/self-hosting#opentelemetry) exposes individual upstream attempts when you need to investigate retries and fallback.

<Cards>
  <Card title="Virtual Models" href="/docs/models-routing/virtual-models" description="Define the named endpoints used by a fallback chain." />
  <Card title="BYOK & Subscriptions" href="/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions" description="Connect the accounts and endpoints in your chain." />
  <Card title="Local Models" href="/docs/models-routing/local-models" description="Add a local inference endpoint." />
</Cards>

content/docs/(guide)/models-routing/virt.content:
---
title: Virtual Models
description: Give configured model endpoints a reusable name, then call that name from an application or harness.
---

A **virtual model** is a named entry under `models` in `bitrouter.yaml`. It exposes configured provider/model endpoints through one callable name, such as `coding`, so an application can keep using that name when you change its backing endpoints.

Connect the sources first with [BYOK & Subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions) or [Local Models](/docs/models-routing/local-models). Use [Model Fallbacks](/docs/models-routing/model-fallback) for the failure conditions and replacement behavior of a multi-endpoint route.

## Define a virtual model

```yaml
models:
  coding:
    strategy: priority
    endpoints:
      - provider: openai
        service_id: gpt-5
      - provider: anthropic
        service_id: claude-sonnet-4-6
```

`coding` is the name callers use. Each endpoint identifies a configured provider and a model id that provider serves. With `strategy: priority`, eligible endpoints are tried in the configured order; [Model Fallbacks](/docs/models-routing/model-fallback#fallback-chains) explains when another endpoint is attempted.

A virtual model defines a named route. It does not by itself evaluate answer quality or introduce an automatic cost optimizer.

## Call the name

Use the virtual model wherever the API accepts a model selector:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:4356/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "coding",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this change."}]
  }'
```

An authenticated deployment also requires a BitRouter credential. A native harness launch can use the same name:

```bash
bro claude --model coding
bro codex --model coding
```

See [bro [harness]](/docs/integration/bro-harness) for launch configuration and [Responses API](/docs/usage/responses-api) for the Responses request format.

## Model selector forms

For hosted Cloud model IDs, use [GET /v1/models](/docs/reference/discovery/listModels). Catalog discovery does not grant account access or guarantee that a provider can serve a particular request.

| Selector | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `coding` | A matching virtual model defined under `models` |
| `openai/gpt-5.4` | A logical model id that may be served by multiple connected providers |
| `openai:openai/gpt-5.4` | An explicit route through one configured provider |
| `bitrouter/fast` | A named local router that supplies model selection and request defaults |
| `@fast` | A compatible legacy preset |
| `@fast:primary` | A preset with a configured variant |
| `bitrouter/auto` | The local `auto` router with a routing-policy binding |

The slash in a logical model id is part of the model's identity; it does not pin the serving provider. The colon form explicitly selects a provider. Subscription sources require an explicit provider-qualified route, as described in [BYOK & Subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions#subscriptions).

## Resolution order

The self-hosted proxy resolves a selector in this order:

1. Resolve a named `bitrouter/<name>` router or a legacy `@preset` with an optional `:variant`.
2. Treat `provider:model` as an explicit provider route.
3. Resolve a matching entry under `models` as a virtual model.
4. Otherwise, resolve the logical model id across active providers that declare it.

Choose a virtual name that does not collide with a logical model id when both should remain separately addressable.

## Presets

A named local router can select a virtual model and add reusable request defaults:

```yaml
routers:
  fast:
    selection:
      kind: model
      model: coding
    defaults:
      system_prompt: "Be concise."
      params:
        temperature: 0.2
```

Call `bitrouter/fast` to apply those defaults. Request fields take precedence. Existing local `@fast` selectors still address legacy presets. Use `bro config migrate-routers --candidate <path>` to preview a migration. Cloud uses catalog model IDs or enabled workspace presets addressed as `@<name>`.

`bitrouter/auto` requires a policy binding on the named local router. See the [Auto Router guide](/docs/routing/auto-router#initialize-a-policy-binding) for initializing that binding.

## Variants

A configured variant applies routing preferences to a selector, for example `coding:private` or `@fast:primary`. It does not create another virtual-model definition. An unknown suffix remains part of the selector instead of being silently removed.

Variants do not grant access, bypass guardrails, or supply provider credentials. Configure candidate filters in [Strategies](/docs/routing/strategies#variants).

## Protocol compatibility

Every endpoint must support the capabilities required by the request. Giving several endpoints one virtual name does not make their tools, structured outputs, or provider continuity interchangeable.

For custom endpoints, declare only verified model capabilities in [BYOK & Subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions#custom-endpoints-and-models). [Responses API](/docs/usage/responses-api#structured-outputs-across-protocols) explains response-format fields across supported protocols. Use a schema supported by every model that may serve a fallback request.

## Inspect and verify

```bash
bro config validate -c bitrouter.yaml
bro route coding -c bitrouter.yaml
bro route bitrouter/fast -c bitrouter.yaml
bro requests --limit 25
```

`bro route` previews resolution without sending an inference request. It uses the running daemon when available and otherwise resolves from the selected configuration file. [Request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts) identify the model and provider that actually served a call.

<Cards>
  <Card title="Model Fallbacks" href="/docs/models-routing/model-fallback" description="Understand replacement order and retryable failures." />
  <Card title="BYOK & Subscriptions" href="/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions" description="Connect the accounts and endpoints behind a virtual model." />
  <Card title="Local Models" href="/docs/models-routing/local-models" description="Add a local inference endpoint." />
  <Card title="Configuration (YAML)" href="/docs/routing/configuration" description="Find, validate, and apply the configuration." />
</Cards>

content/docs/(guide)/overview/comparison.content:
---
title: LiteLLM
description: Compare BitRouter with LiteLLM's SDK and proxy across gateway operations, automatic routing, and migration.
---

[LiteLLM](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/) offers a Python SDK and a self-hosted proxy with provider translation, retries, fallbacks, virtual keys, spend tracking, and administration. It also documents [Auto Routing in beta](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/auto_routing), including classifiers and adaptive model pools. Compare your required integration shape, gateway controls, and policy workflow.

## Key differences

| Question | LiteLLM | BitRouter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How is it integrated? | Python SDK in an application or a separate proxy | Standalone daemon/API and CLI; managed Cloud option |
| What is the gateway surface? | Broad provider/endpoint support and centralized administration | Routed generation, model-source configuration, and supported agent connections |
| How are routing decisions configured? | Deployment strategies and beta classification/adaptive routing | Virtual-model endpoints and a separately bound routing policy |
| How are changes reviewed? | Configure the selected gateway and routing features | Inspect policy-lock changes and explicitly apply reviewed candidates |

BitRouter's [Auto Router](/docs/routing/auto-router) and [Evaluations](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#evaluations) describe runtime outcome observations and objective evaluation evidence separately. LiteLLM's beta adaptive routing also accepts feedback. Having feedback support does not establish that two systems use the same outcome, attribution, or publication rules.

## Choose BitRouter when

- A standalone routing service and CLI fit your operating model.
- You want to inspect and version a policy artifact alongside your deployment configuration.
- You want to connect [API keys, subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions), and [local inference](/docs/models-routing/local-models) through BitRouter's supported routes.

Self-hosted BYOK requests have no BitRouter inference fee. Provider charges and infrastructure costs still apply; BitRouter Cloud has separate managed terms.

## Choose LiteLLM when

- Your application relies on its importable Python SDK and integrations.
- You need its documented endpoint coverage or existing gateway administration workflows.
- You already operate its virtual-key, budget, logging, caching, or enterprise controls and have no replacement requirement.

Check the [current LiteLLM documentation](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/) and [commercial packaging](https://www.litellm.ai/pricing) for the features and deployment edition you use. Compare required capabilities individually before replacing a gateway.

## Migrate from LiteLLM

If you call `litellm.completion` in-process, migration changes application architecture: use a compatible HTTP client against BitRouter. Replacing LiteLLM Proxy can preserve a supported client wire format, but its gateway settings still need translation.

1. Choose [Cloud or a local daemon](/docs/overview/quickstart) and configure the required upstream credentials.
2. Change the client base URL to `https://api.bitrouter.ai/v1` or `http://127.0.0.1:4356/v1`, with the corresponding BitRouter credential.
3. Translate `model_list` aliases and deployments into [Virtual Models](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models), [Strategies](/docs/routing/strategies) constraints, and [Model Fallbacks](/docs/models-routing/model-fallback).
4. If using auto routing, define and validate the destination [policy binding](/docs/routing/auto-router#initialize-a-policy-binding). Existing classifier, tier, or feedback settings do not transfer automatically.
5. Inventory hooks, budgets, keys, caching, non-generation endpoints, and admin dependencies. Keep a workload on its existing gateway until each required capability has a verified replacement.
6. Replay representative requests, inspect settled [receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts), and configure [OpenTelemetry export](/docs/self-hosting#opentelemetry) before retiring the previous proxy.

Use [Chat Completions / Messages](/docs/usage/responses-api#chat-completions) for an existing compatible client or [Responses (default)](/docs/usage/responses-api) for a new integration.

---
title: OpenRouter
description: Compare BitRouter and OpenRouter across model selection, policy ownership, deployment, and migration.
---

OpenRouter offers hosted access to models and providers through one API. Its [Auto Router](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/auto-router) classifies requests by task and ranks models using aggregate market spend, with model restrictions and cost tiers. Both products can choose models automatically; compare the selection signal and who controls the deployed policy.

## Key differences

| Question | OpenRouter | BitRouter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who operates the router? | Hosted service | Self-hosted Apache-2.0 runtime or BitRouter Cloud |
| How is automatic model selection configured? | Auto Router settings and hosted rankings | A policy bound to a preset such as `bitrouter/auto` |
| How are eligible routes constrained? | Model restrictions and [provider preferences](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection) | Configured sources and [Strategies](/docs/routing/strategies) filters |
| How can operators review policy changes? | Configure the service's exposed controls | Inspect a versioned policy lock and explicitly apply reviewed candidates |

BitRouter's [Auto Router](/docs/routing/auto-router) separates model selection from failure-driven fallback. Its [evaluation workflow](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#evaluations) uses admitted objective results and frozen evidence snapshots to assess policy candidates. Collecting traffic or enabling an auto selector alone does not prove that the policy improved your workflow.

## Choose BitRouter when

- You need to run the routing process alongside your own credentials, private endpoints, or local models.
- You want to inspect and version the policy artifact that your deployment uses.
- You can supply representative workflow outcomes and review candidate changes before publication.

Self-hosted BYOK has no BitRouter inference fee; you still pay upstream inference and infrastructure costs. Cloud is a separate managed offering. The [Quickstart](/docs/overview/quickstart) explains both deployment paths.

## Choose OpenRouter when

- You want a hosted catalog and provider access through one account.
- You prefer its managed Auto Router and cost-tier controls.
- Your application already depends on its provider preferences or other hosted features.

Check [OpenRouter pricing](https://openrouter.ai/pricing) for current model rates and BYOK terms. A catalog listing, low token rate, or routing strategy is not a measurement of end-to-end task cost; test your actual workload.

## Migrate from OpenRouter

For a compatible client, replace the base URL and credential:

```diff
- base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1"
- api_key=OPENROUTER_API_KEY
+ base_url="https://api.bitrouter.ai/v1"
+ api_key=BITROUTER_API_KEY
```

For a local daemon, use `http://127.0.0.1:4356/v1` and the authentication configured for that deployment. Configure upstream sources through [BYOK & Subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions) or [Local Models](/docs/models-routing/local-models).

1. Resolve each explicit model id against the destination catalog; matching spellings do not guarantee matching availability or capabilities.
2. For Cloud, choose a catalog model or an enabled workspace routing preset addressed as `@<name>`. For a self-hosted deployment, initialize the [BitRouter auto binding](/docs/routing/auto-router#initialize-a-policy-binding) before using `bitrouter/auto`.
3. Translate provider restrictions, fallback lists, and router/plugin settings into BitRouter's model and routing configuration. Review OpenRouter-specific headers and extensions individually.
4. Replay representative streaming, tool, and structured-output requests. Inspect [Request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts) for the actual serving model, usage, and fallback behavior.

See [Chat Completions / Messages](/docs/usage/responses-api#chat-completions) for existing client formats and [Responses (default)](/docs/usage/responses-api) for a new generation integration.

---
title: Router (Ramp)
description: Compare BitRouter with Ramp Router across managed routing, model evaluation, policy control, and integration.
---

[Router from Ramp](https://docs.router.com/) provides a managed model endpoint with fallbacks, spend tracking, and request inspection. Ramp also describes evaluating models and routing production workloads in its [launch announcement](https://ramp.com/blog/router-launch). The useful comparison is how you select models, evaluate changes, and control deployment.

## Key differences

| Question | Router (Ramp) | BitRouter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What do clients connect to? | Ramp's managed endpoint | Your local/self-hosted daemon or BitRouter Cloud |
| How do clients select routes? | Catalog model ids, provider pins, and ordered fallback lists | Virtual models, logical ids, provider-qualified selectors, or a policy-bound preset |
| What can you inspect? | Request, model, usage, and spend through the service | Settled request receipts and the policy/configuration used by your deployment |
| How do you assess a policy change? | Use the service's supported evaluation and strategy controls | Submit objective evaluation results, freeze evidence, and review a candidate before publication |

Router documents its [model selectors and capability constraints](https://docs.router.com/guides/choose-a-model). BitRouter documents its [Virtual Models](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models), [model-routing mechanics](/docs/routing/strategies), and [evaluation evidence](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#evaluations) so a named endpoint, selection policy, and evaluation result have distinct roles.

A vendor's reported savings describe its own workload and baseline. Measure successful-task cost, quality, retries, and latency on your workload before treating a routing strategy as an improvement.

## Choose BitRouter when

- You need a routing process you can operate on your own infrastructure.
- You want private or local inference sources in your eligible pool.
- You want to version the model-selection policy and explicitly review publication of evidence-derived candidates.

BitRouter's native [Context Routing](/docs/routing/context-routing) also selects evidence for the next model call when its managed runtime owns that task. Proxying an external harness's requests does not transfer ownership of its history to BitRouter.

## Choose Router (Ramp) when

- You prefer Ramp's managed endpoint and request inspection.
- Its supported models, routing strategies, and evaluation workflow fit your application.
- You want to keep an existing Router integration and its account-level operations.

Consult the current [Router documentation](https://docs.router.com/) for availability, limits, supported strategies, and account requirements.

## Migrate from Router (Ramp)

For a Responses-compatible SDK, change the base URL and credential:

```diff
- base_url="https://api.router.com/v1"
- api_key=RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY
+ base_url="https://api.bitrouter.ai/v1"
+ api_key=BITROUTER_API_KEY
```

A local BitRouter daemon uses `http://127.0.0.1:4356/v1` and its configured authentication.

1. Map source catalog ids to configured BitRouter [model selectors](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models#model-selector-forms).
2. Translate ordered alternatives into [Model Fallbacks](/docs/models-routing/model-fallback). Configure [Auto Router](/docs/routing/auto-router) separately if BitRouter should choose a model before execution.
3. Review service-tier pins and provider-specific fields individually; a shared wire format does not make route settings interchangeable.
4. Start a fresh test conversation when moving deployments. Retained response ids belong to the deployment that issued them; see [Responses continuation](/docs/usage/responses-api#continue-a-conversation).
5. Compare representative requests and settled [receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts), including tool calls, streaming, usage, and failure handling.

---
title: vLLM Semantic Router
description: Compare programmable routing signals, model paths, evidence selection, and deployment responsibilities.
---

[vLLM Semantic Router](https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router) is an Apache-2.0 decision layer that selects or combines models across configured backends. It overlaps directly with BitRouter in programmable model routing. Compare the policy and runtime contracts your application needs.

## Key differences

| Question | vLLM Semantic Router | BitRouter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How is behavior expressed? | Entrypoints and recipes with signals and route behavior | Model definitions, policy-bound presets, and versioned policy artifacts |
| What can a route do? | Select a model or compose a bounded model workflow | Select eligible endpoints, apply fallback, and execute supported requests |
| What evidence supports improvement? | Routing metadata, feedback, replay, and evaluation | Settled receipts, objective result admission, and frozen evaluation snapshots |
| Who owns task history? | The external harness owns its agent loop and task state | External harnesses retain ownership; the native managed runtime can own retained evidence and context views |

The project's [architecture introduction](https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router/blob/main/website/docs/intro.md) describes its signals, route behaviors, standalone frontend, optional Envoy integration, and separate model runtime. External inference platforms serve its chat backends. It also exposes System One judgments; decision-model access alone is therefore not a distinguishing feature.

BitRouter's [Strategies](/docs/routing/strategies) explains candidate eligibility and model selection. [Auto Router](/docs/routing/auto-router) covers policy-bound model selection and evidence, while [Context Routing](/docs/routing/context-routing) selects evidence supplied to the next call. Native context views depend on runtime/build support and require ownership of the retained evidence.

## Choose BitRouter when

- You want the BitRouter daemon and CLI as the operating surface for model sources, routes, and request receipts.
- You want to manage a preset-bound model policy and explicitly review candidate publication.
- You need the native managed runtime's retained-evidence operations and can validate that runtime for your task.

The [evaluation guide](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#evaluations) describes which results can enter BitRouter's evidence store. A classification result, a routing log, and an objective task outcome are different kinds of evidence.

## Choose vLLM Semantic Router when

- You want its recipe and signal system for model selection or bounded multi-model workflows.
- Its separation of frontend, model runtime, and inference backends fits your deployment.
- Your harness should keep task state while a programmable layer controls each model call.

Both projects offer open-source routing. Compare the components you will operate and the policy behavior you can reproduce on your workload. This page makes no latency, quality, or cost ranking between them.

## Plan a migration

1. Inventory the current entrypoints, signals, recipes, and route behaviors. Record which ones are required by the application.
2. Connect the same usable backends through [BYOK & Subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions) or [Local Models](/docs/models-routing/local-models), then define BitRouter [Virtual Models](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models).
3. Recreate model-selection and fallback behavior using BitRouter's documented controls. Recipe actions and bounded multi-model workflows need an explicit replacement in the application or runtime; changing the base URL does not translate them.
4. Keep the harness responsible for its history unless you explicitly adopt a native task runtime. Test tools, continuation, and context handling in that ownership model.
5. Replay a fixed workload and compare task outcomes, full execution cost, latency, and failure recovery before switching traffic.

Use [Responses (default)](/docs/usage/responses-api) or [Chat Completions / Messages](/docs/usage/responses-api#chat-completions) for the destination client contract.

---
title: Elastic Inference
description: Trade inference across price, time, and heterogeneous models.
---

<Callout type="info">
Elastic Inference is an optional BitRouter Cloud service. BitRouter OSS works independently without it. See [Auto Router](/docs/routing/auto-router) to route requests using your own inference sources.
</Callout>

<a id="what-is-flex-inference" />

## What is Elastic Inference?

Elastic Inference brings three dimensions into each purchasing decision:

- **Price.** Set a maximum total spend for your request. BitRouter compares eligible offers using estimated charges, while checking that their maximum authorized charges fit your budget.
- **Time.** Request immediate purchasing or allow BitRouter to seek opportunities within a purchase window. For cost-focused requests, you can authorize waiting for a potentially cheaper opportunity.
- **Heterogeneous models.** Keep one model fixed or specify several acceptable alternatives. BitRouter compares eligible sources across that selection and purchases one option for the request.

Cache affinity informs source selection: opportunities to reuse context can affect expected cost and latency alongside published rates and available capacity.

You control the acceptable range. BitRouter makes purchasing decisions within it.

Elastic Inference uses **$0.01 per million processed tokens — early access pricing**. Processed tokens are actual input + output tokens. The Cloud platform fee is added to the supplier’s actual inference charge and counted once per request, including when Auto Routing selects Elastic Inference. Your total price cap includes both charges. See [pricing](/pricing).

<a id="why-flex-inference" />

## Why Elastic Inference?

We believe using tokens should feel as effortless as using electricity. You should be able to focus on the work you want done, without constantly comparing providers, checking prices, and deciding where every request should go.

Behind that simple experience, there should be a market. Just as electricity has exchanges, inference should have a place where demand and available supply can meet.

Fixed-price tiers provide a simple way to purchase inference, but they leave limited room to express the flexibility of an individual request. One task needs an immediate response from a specific model. Another accepts several models and can wait for a lower-cost opportunity. Their purchasing needs are different.

Elastic Inference makes those differences actionable. You express your requirements and preferences, and BitRouter handles the purchasing decisions within them.

## How it works

Each limit order defines the terms under which you authorize a trade. A buyer limits the total charge for one complete request; a seller publishes rates and service conditions for eligible requests.

### Buy limit orders

| Order | Acceptable models | Total price cap | Timing and preference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Buy now | Model A | $0.05 | Immediately seek the lowest estimated cost; close if unfilled |
| Allow cost flexibility | Model A or B | $0.05 | Keep open for one hour; allow waiting for a lower-cost opportunity |
| Favor earlier completion | Model A or B | $0.05 | Purchase immediately; prefer the earliest estimated completion |

The first and third orders use **Immediate or Cancel (IOC)**: one bounded purchasing round, without waiting for future offers. The second uses **Good Till Date (GTD)**: it remains open until its expiry, with separate permission to wait for a lower-cost opportunity. GTD can also purchase immediately.

The following JSON illustrates the second order. `50000` micro-USD is **$0.05**, and the expiry is one hour after the example entry time of `1793000000000` Unix milliseconds.

<Callout type="info">
These payloads illustrate the order design. Field names are provisional and are not a released API contract. Model and service references are placeholders.
</Callout>

```json
{
  "client_order_id": "summarize-001",
  "idempotency_key": "submit-summarize-001",
  "request": {
    "request_ref": "request/summary/001",
    "request_digest": "digest/summary/001",
    "max_output_tokens": 2048
  },
  "acceptable_models": ["model-a", "model-b"],
  "side": "buy",
  "order_type": "limit",
  "price_cap_micro_usd": 50000,
  "time_in_force": {
    "kind": "gtd",
    "expires_at_ms": 1793003600000
  },
  "strategy": {
    "selection_objective": "lowest_estimated_cost",
    "timing_policy": "allow_cost_wait",
    "version": 1
  }
}
```

BitRouter compares eligible offers for both models and may purchase immediately or wait and reassess. The order authorizes one selected option. A candidate qualifies only when its maximum authorized charge, including the Cloud platform fee calculated using input tokens and the full output limit, fits the cap; a lower estimated charge alone is insufficient.

### Sell limit offer

A provider can publish a standing offer with rates and service conditions:

| Term | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Model | Model A |
| Input rate | $0.20 per million tokens |
| Cached-input rate | $0.05 per million tokens |
| Output rate | $0.80 per million tokens |
| Offer validity | 30 minutes |
| Service conditions | The published conditions for the referenced request-size profile |
| Repeat sales | Allowed while the offer is valid and capacity is available |

The corresponding JSON uses micro-USD per million tokens. Its expiry is 30 minutes after the same example entry time.

```json
{
  "offer_id": "offer-model-a-small",
  "side": "sell",
  "order_type": "limit",
  "supply_mode": "standing",
  "revision": 7,
  "deployment_ref": "deployment/model-a@3",
  "request_profile_ref": "request-profile/small@1",
  "pricing": {
    "metering_ref": "llm-three-rates@1",
    "input_micro_usd_per_mtok": 200000,
    "cache_input_micro_usd_per_mtok": 50000,
    "output_micro_usd_per_mtok": 800000
  },
  "service_conditions_ref": "quick-delivery/small@1",
  "time_in_force": {
    "kind": "gtd",
    "expires_at_ms": 1793001800000
  }
}
```

Each acceptance checks the request against the offer's scope, service conditions, and available capacity. Input, cached-input, and output rates determine the supplier charge. The maximum buyer charge also includes the Cloud platform fee for input tokens plus the full output limit and must fit the buyer's cap. At early access pricing, a request processing 3,000 input + 1,000 output tokens incurs a $0.00004 platform fee, in addition to its actual supplier charge. The platform fee is based on processed tokens and counted once per request, rather than on the supplier charge, budget cap, or top-up amount.

*All prices, durations, and identifiers above are illustrative.*

An order’s validity determines when a new trade may be accepted. **It does not specify when inference must finish.** Once accepted, the provider proceeds under the agreed service terms, and charges follow actual metered usage. Waiting does not guarantee a cheaper offer or a successful trade.

## What’s next?

Buyers define what they need and the terms they accept. Providers offer inference capacity with published pricing and service conditions. BitRouter connects eligible offers with requests.

- [Price-Time Priority](/docs/market/price-time-priority) — understand purchase timing, price caps, and Cloud platform fees.
- [Inference Types](/docs/market/inference-types) — compare On-demand, Interruptible, and Reserved capacity. Reserved is Coming soon.
- [Inference Tiers](/docs/market/inference-tiers) — compare Unverified, Verified, and Secured inference in the market design.
- [Buy Inference](/docs/market/buy-inference) — buyer guide and pricing boundaries.
- [Sell Inference](/docs/market/sell-inference) — supplier guide and pricing boundaries.

content/docs/(guide)/overview/quickstart.content:
---
title: Quickstart
description: Install BitRouter and get your agent routing in under a minute — pick self-host or Cloud, then onboard via the Agent Skill, the CLI wizard, or manual env keys.
---

This page gets BitRouter routing for your agent in under a minute. There are two deployment modes, and three ways to onboard either one — the Agent Skill, the CLI wizard, or manual env keys.

- **BitRouter Cloud (default).** Hosted endpoint at `api.bitrouter.ai`. Cloud Auto Routing with your own provider keys and Elastic Inference share $0.01 per million processed input + output tokens at early access pricing. Each request is counted once. Provider or supplier inference charges are separate.
- **Local proxy.** A single binary on your machine, BYOK with your own provider keys. Basic routing requires no external service.

For a hosted API integration, start with [Cloud authentication and your first request](#authenticate-and-send-your-first-request).

Both modes use the **same open-source routing core** (Apache 2.0). The deployment boundary changes, but the client protocol does not, so you can switch modes without rewriting your harness.

## Self-host or Cloud?

The routing contract is shared, while operational surfaces follow the deployment boundary:

- **Self-host** if you already have provider keys, run local/private models, have data-residency rules, or are prototyping solo.
- **Cloud** if you want BitRouter to operate the router and provide hosted model access.

| Capability | Self-hosted (OSS) | Cloud |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Universal API + cross-protocol routing | ✅ | ✅ |
| Local / private model endpoints | ✅ | — |
| Model fallback & provider selection | ✅ | ✅ |
| Model variants & presets | ✅ | ✅ |
| Local evidence-based routing policies | ✅ | — |
| Request checks / guardrails | Custom host | ✅ |
| OTLP trace + metric export | ✅ | — |
| Local MCP gateway & server tools | ✅ | — |
| Local ACP adapters | ✅ | — |
| Structured outputs | ✅ | ✅ |
| Namespace isolation primitive | ✅ | ✅ |
| Managed provider network (no upstream keys needed) | — | ✅ |
| Hosted activity and request receipts | — | ✅ |
| Elastic Inference (supplier charges + Cloud platform usage) | — | ✅ |
| Cloud Auto Routing with BYOK (same Cloud platform usage) | — | ✅ |

Self-hosted request checks require a [compiled extension in a custom host](https://github.com/bitrouter/bitrouter/blob/main/docs/GUARDRAILS_EXTENSION.md); the default `bro` binary does not include a matcher.

BitRouter does not package a separate enterprise suite today. Teams with deployment, security, procurement, or support requirements can [contact the founders](mailto:contact@bitrouter.ai) and help shape the team offering.

Do you need your own provider keys? Cloud BYOK uses your provider credentials; the provider bills inference separately. Elastic Inference purchases supplier inference through BitRouter. Both use the same Cloud platform fee of $0.01 per million processed input + output tokens at early access pricing, counted once per request. You can attach Cloud to a self-hosted binary and use both. Self-hosted routing remains free of BitRouter fees. See [pricing](/pricing).

## Install the binary

<Tabs items={['macOS / Linux', 'Homebrew', 'npm', 'cargo']}>
<Tab value="macOS / Linux">

```bash
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://github.com/bitrouter/bitrouter/releases/download/v1.0.0-alpha.33/bitrouter-installer.sh | sh
```

</Tab>
<Tab value="Homebrew">

```bash
brew install bitrouter/tap/bitrouter
```

</Tab>
<Tab value="npm">

```bash
npm install -g bitrouter
```

</Tab>
<Tab value="cargo">

```bash
cargo install bitrouter
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Use BitRouter Cloud

### Authenticate and send your first request

1. Sign in to your account at the [BitRouter Cloud console](https://cloud.bitrouter.ai/sign-in).
2. After [installing the CLI](#install-the-binary), sign in from the terminal and mint a key with the `inference:invoke` scope:

```bash
bro cloud login
bro cloud keys mint --name my-integration --scope inference:invoke
```

`bro cloud login` uses a browser device sign-in flow. Follow the displayed URL and code to complete it.
The mint command prints the new key once. Replace the placeholder below with that key:

```bash
export BITROUTER_API_KEY='paste-your-cloud-key-here'
```

3. Send a Responses API request directly to the hosted Cloud endpoint:

```bash
curl https://api.bitrouter.ai/v1/responses \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BITROUTER_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5","input":"Hello!"}'
```

The Cloud API host is `https://api.bitrouter.ai`; the SDK base URL is `https://api.bitrouter.ai/v1`.
Use a [Cloud catalog model ID](/docs/reference/discovery/listModels) that your account can access, or an enabled workspace routing preset.
The local `bitrouter/auto` selector requires a self-hosted policy binding.
See [Cloud authentication](/docs/reference/authentication#cloud-api-keys), the [Python client example](/docs/reference#python-client), and the [Responses API contract](/docs/reference/openai-responses/createResponse).

### Use Cloud through a local proxy

After `bro cloud login`, run `bro start`. The `bitrouter` provider auto-enables once signed in, so Cloud-managed models can be routed alongside your BYOK keys through `http://127.0.0.1:4356/v1`.
The direct Cloud request above does not require a local proxy.

Cloud BYOK uses your provider keys, with inference billed by the provider. Elastic Inference bills supplier inference charges through BitRouter.
Both share a Cloud platform fee of $0.01 per million processed input + output tokens at early access pricing, counted once per request. See [pricing](/pricing).

## Onboard via the Agent Skill

For agent runtimes that support skills (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Copilot, etc.). BitRouter ships a `/bitrouter` [Agent Skill](https://agentskills.io) so the agent can install, configure, migrate to, and troubleshoot BitRouter **on its own** — the skill carries the facts that drift easily (the listen port, env var names, the `provider/model` slash form, which subcommands exist), and it lives in the main repo at `skills/bitrouter/`, kept in sync with the code in the same change. Install once:

```bash
npx skills add bitrouter/bitrouter    # via the generic skills CLI
```

Then ask your agent: *"Set up BitRouter for me."* — the agent runs the wizard, picks Cloud by default, and verifies the connection autonomously.

<Callout type="info">
The `/bitrouter` Skill explains which structured `bro` command to use. The agent host still owns approval and execution; BitRouter does not publish the local skill directory as an MCP origin server.
</Callout>

## Onboard via the CLI wizard

For terminal-first setup, launch the wizard:

```bash
bro
```

Bare `bro` opens the saved default agent when one is configured; otherwise, in a terminal, it starts the wizard and probes local credentials. After setup, it can open the configured TUI conversation. The wizard walks three steps:

1. **Credentials** — sign in to BitRouter Cloud (default), log in to a provider, or paste a BYOK key.
2. **Harness** — choose a default ACP adapter. Adapters use a compatible local CLI when available.
3. **Finish** — open BitRouter Code, start the proxy at `http://127.0.0.1:4356`, or exit.

Every step maps to a flag, so an agent or CI can configure BitRouter without a human. With `--yes`, the wizard consumes flag-supplied credentials, reports and skips interactive OAuth, and emits a JSON result envelope on stdout. Select `--after exit` to finish without opening Code or starting the proxy:

```bash
bro init --yes --provider openai --provider-api-key "sk-..." --harness claude --after serve
bro init --yes --use-detected --harness claude --after serve   # accept env keys, run proxy
bro init --yes --api-key "brk_..." --after exit                # Cloud key, no launch
bro init --reset                                               # clear credentials, start over
```

Every flag is documented in the [`bro init` reference](/docs/usage/cli#bro-init). The wizard creates or updates the resolved `bitrouter.yaml`, recording the selected agent, optional model, and provider entries. Without `--force` it starts from the existing configuration; `--force` starts from the starter template.

## Run self-hosted

Set your provider keys in the environment and start the proxy:

```bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...    # ANTHROPIC_API_KEY / GEMINI_API_KEY also work
bro start
# Proxy running at http://127.0.0.1:4356
```

BitRouter auto-detects any key set in the environment — no config file needed. Any provider whose key is present is immediately available. See [BYOK](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions#built-in-providers-with-your-own-key) for the full list of recognized variables, or [local inference](/docs/models-routing/local-models) to point BitRouter at Ollama, vLLM, or LM Studio for free.

For advanced routing rules or multi-account failover, scaffold a config file:

```bash
bro init -c ./bitrouter.yaml  # choose an explicit destination
bro start
```

## Point your agent at the proxy

However you start it, BitRouter is a drop-in proxy. Point your agent runtime at the proxy base URL — `http://127.0.0.1:4356` when self-hosting — and every model call routes through BitRouter with no harness changes.

Verify with a request:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:4356/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "openai/gpt-4o",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]
  }'
```

Point any OpenAI-compatible runtime at `http://127.0.0.1:4356/v1` to route through BitRouter.

Two commands make the routing decision itself legible:

```bash
bro models                            # every model id routable right now
bro route anthropic/claude-opus-4.8   # preview the routing decision
```

Model selectors use two similar-looking forms for different jobs:

| Form | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `provider/model` | Stable logical model id; BitRouter may route it through any eligible provider | `anthropic/claude-opus-4.8` |
| `provider:model` | Explicit provider pin for local routing | `anthropic:anthropic/claude-opus-4.8` |

Use the slash form by default. Use the colon form only when you intentionally need one configured provider, such as a subscription-backed route. See [Virtual Models](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models#model-selector-forms) for the complete resolution order.

## Adaptive routing

Explicit model ids give you deterministic model selection. To let a self-hosted router apply the policy bound to its named `auto` router, keep one stable model id in your agent or application:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:4356/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "bitrouter/auto", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "..."}]}'
```

`bitrouter/auto` requires an `auto` policy binding and fails visibly when the binding is missing. The [Auto Router guide](/docs/routing/auto-router#initialize-a-policy-binding) shows how to create it, inspect the selected route, and publish a reviewed policy update. Cloud uses catalog model IDs or enabled workspace routing presets such as `@<name>`; it does not use this local selector. [Evaluations](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#evaluations) covers objective-scored evidence.

## Next steps

<Cards>
  <Card title="Virtual Models" href="/docs/models-routing/virtual-models" description="Define named model endpoints and request profiles." />
  <Card title="bitrouter/auto" href="/docs/routing/auto-router#initialize-a-policy-binding" description="Use one stable model id and inspect the policy-driven route." />
