content/docs/(guide)/overview/what-is-bi.content:
---
title: How BitRouter Works
description: Route model requests through an inspectable policy and use evidence to improve your agent workflows.
---

**BitRouter is a context-aware LLM router for agent workflows.** In a self-hosted deployment, a configured `bitrouter/auto` router selects models using a policy you can inspect, review, and update from admitted evidence.

Agents can browse the [documentation index](/llms.txt), connect to the public [documentation MCP endpoint](/mcp) over Streamable HTTP to search docs and look up models, or read the [BitRouter Cloud OpenAPI schema](/openapi.json).

Model prices and capabilities change. BitRouter helps operators compare routes against their own workload and publish reviewed policy changes; evaluating a workload still requires an external evaluator or benchmark.

On a strict 80-task common-valid Terminal-Bench 2.1 comparison, an initial BitRouter configuration reached **81.25% task success** versus **81.56%** for a fixed strong-model baseline and **76.50%** for same-pool random routing. Its frozen-price nominal API cost for accepted valid-path requests was **40.93% lower** than the strong-model baseline. These are research results, not provider billing or an official leaderboard submission; review the [data and protocol](https://huggingface.co/datasets/BitRouterAI/benchmarks).

## A self-hosted model id for policy routing

Two things change — the base URL, and the model you ask for:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:4356/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "bitrouter/auto", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "..."}]}'
```

Explicit model ids select that model and can still use eligible provider fallback. Cloud accepts catalog model IDs and enabled workspace routing presets addressed as `@<name>`; its hosted endpoint does not use the local `bitrouter/auto` selector.

The local router can classify request context and resolve it against a versioned policy. Its configured tiers and explicit routes determine which model is selected; unmatched requests use the policy's default tier.

The local `bitrouter/auto` selector needs a bound policy before first use; an unbound install reports the missing binding. Follow the [setup guide](/docs/routing/auto-router) before sending the example.

## Use traffic and evaluations as evidence

The self-hosted workflow combines routing with telemetry, evaluation, and explicit policy publication:

- **Act — the router.** Resolve eligible model routes and fall back on retryable failures.
- **Observe — telemetry.** Inspect available request, usage, cost, and outcome records.
- **Evaluate — the objective.** Submit results from an evaluator suited to the workload.
- **Learn — the policy engine.** Use admitted evidence to derive and review a candidate policy.

In alpha.33, the active lock controls request-time routes in both policy modes; legacy live adequacy learning is disabled. You can compile and review a candidate before publishing in adaptive mode. Running the optimizer is a separate authorization that can publish a controller transition.

## It optimizes the workflow, not the request

Every other gateway's unit of optimization is the request: pick a model, return a response, done. BitRouter's unit is the workflow — the whole run, judged on whether it did the job you wanted.

For workflow-level evaluation, run a benchmark or evaluator appropriate to your task and admit its results into the evidence store. The [evaluation guide](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#evaluations) explains the subject, result, and snapshot boundaries.

Use the compile and publish workflow to review a candidate before activating it. Policy rollback can restore an earlier lock by digest.

Use [Integrations](/docs/integration/coding-agents) to connect a native harness to BitRouter. The harness retains its own history, tools, and permissions; BitRouter routes the model requests it receives. The [CLI Getting Started](/docs/cli/getting-started) covers terminal setup and entry points.

The Core is Apache 2.0 and free to self-host; Cloud adds managed providers and account-wide policies on top. [Quickstart](/docs/overview/quickstart) has the split.

## Next steps

<Cards>
  <Card title="Quickstart" href="/docs/overview/quickstart" description="Self-host or Cloud, routing in under a minute." />
  <Card title="Use bitrouter/auto" href="/docs/routing/auto-router#initialize-a-policy-binding" description="Run policy-driven traffic, inspect its route, and publish reviewed changes." />
  <Card title="Integrations" href="/docs/integration/coding-agents" description="Run supported harnesses interactively, headlessly, or in their native interface." />
  <Card title="OpenRouter" href="/docs/overview/comparison/openrouter" description="Compare hosted model access and routing policy ownership." />
  <Card title="Router (Ramp)" href="/docs/overview/comparison/router-ramp" description="Compare managed routing, evaluation, and deployment control." />
  <Card title="vLLM Semantic Router" href="/docs/overview/comparison/vllm-semantic-router" description="Compare programmable routing signals and runtime responsibilities." />
  <Card title="LiteLLM" href="/docs/overview/comparison/litellm" description="Compare SDK and proxy integration, routing, and gateway operations." />
</Cards>

content/docs/(guide)/routing/auto-router.content:
---
title: Auto Router
description: Set up bitrouter/auto, send policy-bound requests, override one call, and inspect the serving route.
---

Use the self-hosted `bitrouter/auto` selector when a bound policy should select the model for each request. Connect usable inference sources first, initialize the policy binding, then inspect the serving route and review evidence before publishing policy changes.

[Strategies](/docs/routing/strategies) explains selector resolution, candidate eligibility, and named variants. [Configuration (YAML)](/docs/routing/configuration) covers file discovery, validation, and reload. Automatic model selection remains separate from [Model Fallbacks](/docs/models-routing/model-fallback) after a retryable failure.

Use [Routing Traces](/docs/routing/routing-traces) to follow the router's decisions, serving models, and upstream attempts across the available workflow trajectory.

## Local and Cloud pricing

Self-hosting the OSS router has no BitRouter fee. Cloud Auto Routing and Elastic Inference share **$0.01 per million processed tokens — early access pricing**. Actual input + output tokens are counted once per request, including when Auto Routing selects Elastic Inference. Your provider or supplier charges for model inference separately. Enterprise terms are custom. See [pricing](/pricing).

## Routing rules

<a id="choose-a-strategy" />
<a id="ordered-endpoints" />
<a id="candidate-based-selection" />
<a id="policy-bound-selection" />
<a id="customize-a-strategy" />
<a id="request-presets" />
<a id="variants" />
<a id="ordering-and-release-limits" />

To constrain candidate providers, reuse preferences with `variants:`, or choose ordered endpoints instead of policy-bound selection, use [Strategies](/docs/routing/strategies#choose-a-routing-approach). Its examples cover [request presets](/docs/routing/strategies#request-presets), [variants](/docs/routing/strategies#variants), and [ordering limits](/docs/routing/strategies#ordering-and-release-limits).

<a id="policy-tiers-and-runtime-adequacy" />

## Policy tiers and evidence

Initialize a binding with usable models for its tiers. An unmatched fingerprint uses the configured default tier. In alpha.33, legacy request-time adequacy learning is disabled. [Workload Optimization](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#let-evidence-improve-the-policy) explains how to use admitted evidence to update the policy.

Context-view selection has separate runtime rules. The model policy lock does not configure an external harness's history, and this page does not introduce unsupported context-strategy YAML. See [Context Routing](/docs/routing/context-routing).

## Initialize a policy binding

`bitrouter/auto` uses the routing policy bound to the named `auto` router. An explicit logical model id selects that model while retaining eligible provider fallback; a provider-qualified id pins one provider. Automatic selection and failure-driven fallback are separate decisions.

For a local deployment, initialize the policy binding with two active `provider:model` routes available in your deployment:

```bash
bro policy init auto --router auto \
  --strong openai:openai/gpt-5.6-sol \
  --economy moonshotai:moonshotai/kimi-k2.7-code
bro policy check
bro route bitrouter/auto
```

The initializer writes `policy-lock.yaml` and updates `bitrouter.yaml` while preserving the configured policy mode. The local endpoint fails visibly if the binding is missing. Hosted callers use a catalog model ID or an enabled workspace routing preset addressed as `@<name>`. A hosted preset can supply its own model or accept one as `@<name>/<base-model>`.

Use the selector in an API request or native harness launch:

```bash
bro claude --model bitrouter/auto
bro codex --model bitrouter/auto
```

[Responses API](/docs/usage/responses-api) shows a routed generation request. Inspect the actual serving model with [Request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts); a selector preview does not prove which fallback ultimately served the call.

## Override one call

Use an explicit selector when the caller should choose the model for one invocation:

```bash
bro claude --model openai/gpt-5.4
bro codex --model openai:openai/gpt-5.4
```

An explicit logical id retains eligible provider alternatives. A provider-qualified id also pins the provider. See [Virtual Models](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models#model-selector-forms) for selector resolution and named endpoint definitions.

<a id="let-evidence-improve-the-policy" />
<a id="review-and-publish-a-change" />
<a id="evaluations" />
<a id="two-evidence-paths" />
<a id="evidence-lifecycle" />
<a id="1-define-and-seal-a-subject" />
<a id="2-evaluate-outside-the-router" />
<a id="3-submit-the-result" />
<a id="4-freeze-a-snapshot" />
<a id="5-consume-the-evidence-explicitly" />
<a id="reproducibility-boundary" />
<a id="what-evaluation-does-not-establish" />

## Review evidence and policy changes

[Workload Optimization](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#existing-policy-tools) documents objective-scored [evaluations](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#evaluations), reproducible evidence snapshots, and the [reviewed publication workflow](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#review-and-publish-a-change). Evidence collection does not automatically publish a policy candidate.

<a id="verify-and-apply-a-strategy" />

## Verify and apply the policy

```bash
bro config validate -c bitrouter.yaml
bro route bitrouter/auto -c bitrouter.yaml
bro policy check -c bitrouter.yaml
bro requests --limit 25
```

Use `policy check` to inspect the binding used by `bitrouter/auto`. For other selectors and candidate constraints, use [Strategies](/docs/routing/strategies). Route previews do not send inference or establish task quality; settled [Request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts) show what actually served a call. Apply configuration changes through [Configuration (YAML)](/docs/routing/configuration#apply-and-review-changes), and publish policy candidates through the [review workflow](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#review-and-publish-a-change).

<Cards>
  <Card title="Workload Optimization" href="/docs/routing/workload-optimization" description="Coming soon: learn from recurring workloads to refine routing toward quality, cost, and latency goals." />
  <Card title="Strategies" href="/docs/routing/strategies" description="Understand selector resolution, candidate constraints, and named routing variants." />
  <Card title="Configuration (YAML)" href="/docs/routing/configuration" description="Load, validate, and apply routing configuration." />
  <Card title="Routing Traces" href="/docs/routing/routing-traces" description="Trace routing decisions, serving models, and upstream attempts across a workflow." />
</Cards>

content/docs/(guide)/routing/configurati.content:
---
title: Configuration (YAML)
description: Find the active BitRouter configuration, resolve secrets, validate settings, and apply changes.
---

{/* GENERATED by scripts/generate-config.mjs. Edit config-reference/guide.md or config-reference/index.md, or refresh the pinned schema; do not edit this page. */}

Use `bitrouter.yaml` to connect inference sources, define callable models, and bind routing policies in a local BitRouter deployment. Keep non-secret settings in version control and reference secret values from the environment. A deployment can use in-memory defaults, but an explicit file makes its behavior reproducible.

For a complete field lookup, use [config reference](/docs/routing/configuration#configuration-reference): the pinned schema, required fields, declared defaults, environment references, and reload boundaries. This page starts with the configuration workflow and includes the complete field reference below.

## Configuration and policy artifacts

| Artifact | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `bitrouter.yaml` | Provider connections, virtual models, named routers, legacy presets, variants, and links to routing-policy artifacts |
| `policy-lock.yaml` | Versioned model-selection policy, tier assignments, and adequacy inputs for compilation |

A named router supplies model selection and defaults. A policy binding connects that router to a versioned selection policy. A valid configuration file alone does not create the binding required by `bitrouter/auto`.

[Strategies](/docs/routing/strategies) explains candidate eligibility and selection. [Auto Router](/docs/routing/auto-router) covers policy-bound model selection. [Workload Optimization](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#existing-policy-tools) covers evidence and reviewed publication. [Context Routing](/docs/routing/context-routing) describes native evidence views; this guide does not imply that every context-view rule has a public YAML setting.

## Create a configuration

```bash
bro init -c ./bitrouter.yaml
bro config validate -c bitrouter.yaml
```

```yaml
server:
  listen: "127.0.0.1:4356"
providers:
  openai:
    api_key: "${OPENAI_API_KEY}"
```

Use the guide for the setting you need:

| Task | Guide |
| --- | --- |
| Add an API key, subscription, or custom endpoint | [BYOK & Subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions) |
| Define named endpoints and reusable request defaults | [Virtual Models](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models) |
| Initialize an auto policy | [Auto Router](/docs/routing/auto-router) |
| Evaluate evidence and review policy changes | [Workload Optimization](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#existing-policy-tools) |
| Restrict candidates or reuse named routing variants | [Strategies](/docs/routing/strategies#configure-routing-rules) |
| Define failure-driven replacement routes | [Model Fallbacks](/docs/models-routing/model-fallback) |
| Connect an upstream MCP server | [MCP configuration fields](/docs/routing/configuration#agents-and-mcp) |
| Configure a custom ACP adapter | [Agent configuration fields](/docs/routing/configuration#acp-agent-config) |
| Deploy the process and export telemetry | [Self-hosting](/docs/self-hosting) |

## Find the active configuration

BitRouter uses the first matching source:

| Order | Location | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `-c/--config <PATH>` | Explicit; a missing file is an error |
| 2 | `./bitrouter.yaml` | Project-local configuration |
| 3 | `$BITROUTER_HOME/bitrouter.yaml` | Required when `BITROUTER_HOME` is set |
| 4 | `~/.bitrouter/bitrouter.yaml` | Per-user default configuration |
| 5 | No file | In-memory zero-config defaults |

<Callout type="warning">
If `BITROUTER_HOME` is set but contains no `bitrouter.yaml`, BitRouter stops instead of silently loading another file.
</Callout>

Use `${NAME}` for required environment variables and `${NAME:-default}` for an optional fallback:

```yaml
providers:
  local:
    api_base: "${LOCAL_LLM_URL:-http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1}"
    api_key: "${LOCAL_LLM_KEY}"
```

Environment references inside YAML comments are ignored. The resolved value participates in the running policy, but the secret itself should not be committed.

## Validate the contract

Point a YAML-aware editor at the schema generated from the binary's config types:

```yaml
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bitrouter/bitrouter/main/dist/schema/bitrouter.config.schema.json
```

Pin `main` to a release tag when the file must match a deployed binary exactly. Then validate both syntax and route behavior:

```bash
bro config validate -c bitrouter.yaml
bro route bitrouter/auto -c bitrouter.yaml
bro policy check -c bitrouter.yaml
```

- `config validate` checks the complete router policy without requiring live provider credentials.
- `route` previews model resolution without sending an inference request.
- `policy check` cross-validates the policy file and its linked routing-policy lock.

## Apply and review changes

```bash
bro reload -c bitrouter.yaml
bro policy status -c bitrouter.yaml
bro status -c bitrouter.yaml
```

`reload` applies reloadable changes while the daemon is running. Restart for process-bound changes when the command reports that a field cannot be reloaded. For production rollout, validate and preview the policy with the same released binary that will serve it.

For process supervision, authentication, reload boundaries, and rollback, see [Self-hosting operations](/docs/self-hosting#operate). Use [Request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts) to inspect actual serving routes after applying a change.

A linked `policy-lock.yaml` controls policy-bound model selection; it is separate from caller access-control policy. Validate a policy binding with `bro policy check` rather than treating a valid YAML file as proof that the binding is usable.

## Configuration reference

Use this reference to look up the accepted shape of `bitrouter.yaml`. Start with [Configuration (YAML)](/docs/routing/configuration) to find, create, validate, and apply a file. For connecting a coding agent, use [bro [harness]](/docs/integration/bro-harness).

### Version and scope

The field tables are generated from the **1.0.0-alpha.33 configuration schema**, pinned to [BitRouter source `54c822a34d4d`](https://github.com/bitrouter/bitrouter/blob/54c822a34d4dbfd75d484ca35e108b497048efef/dist/schema/bitrouter.config.schema.json) (source commit dated 2026-10-16). This is a source/schema snapshot, not a claim that every installed binary supports these fields. Check `bro --version` and validate with the binary that will run the file. The [CLI reference](/docs/usage/cli#command-reference) has its own captured command version.

[Download the pinned JSON Schema](/schemas/bitrouter.config.schema.json) for an editor or offline validation. The schema describes file structure; runtime validation, credentials, model capabilities, and policy bindings can impose additional requirements.

```yaml
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://bitrouter.ai/schemas/bitrouter.config.schema.json
```

This site URL serves the snapshot documented here and can change with a docs update. Save the schema locally, or use the commit-pinned source link above, when matching an older deployment.

**Reading the tables:** `Required` applies to the containing object or tagged alternative. `Not declared` means the schema does not publish a default; it does not mean the field is required, disabled, or empty. A schema `null` default is distinct from an inherited or resolved runtime value. Map keys such as provider and agent ids are user-defined; follow the linked type to inspect each value's fields. Types and enum values reflect the pinned schema.

<Callout type="warning">
Schema defaults and onboarding defaults differ. The schema declares `server.listen: "0.0.0.0:4356"` and `server.skip_auth: false`. The local configuration written by `bro init` uses `127.0.0.1:4356` with `skip_auth: true`. Inspect your actual file before assuming a listener or authentication mode. Neither setting grants access to the separate control or task APIs.
</Callout>

### Find a setting

| What you are configuring | Root fields | Usage guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Listener, authentication, upstream timeouts, and storage | `server`, `upstream`, `database` | [Self-hosting](/docs/self-hosting) |
| Provider keys, multiple accounts, and custom endpoints | `providers`, `registry`, `inherit_defaults` | [BYOK & Subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions) |
| Named model endpoints and request defaults | `models`, `presets`, `variants` | [Virtual Models](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models) |
| Named routers, policy artifacts, and checks | `routers`, `policy`, `checkers` | [Workload Optimization](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#existing-policy-tools) |
| Native semantic decision backend | `decision_model` | [Context Routing](/docs/routing/context-routing) |
| ACP adapters and saved interactive defaults | `agents`, `chat` | [Agent configuration fields](/docs/routing/configuration#acp-agent-config) |
| Upstream MCP connections and aggregation | `mcp_servers`, `mcp` | [MCP configuration fields](/docs/routing/configuration#agents-and-mcp) |
| Retention, recording, and continuation | `trajectory`, `acp_recording`, `continuation` | [Request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts) |

Native harness launch prepares connection settings for the child process. `agents` configures ACP adapters; it is not a replacement for the harness's own configuration. See [native launch settings](/docs/integration/bro-harness#what-gets-configured) for that boundary.

`plugins` is an open map whose values are arbitrary JSON; this schema does not define a universal plugin contract. `server_tools` and its supporting types are retained in the schema tables for completeness while their product guides are retired during refactoring. Their presence does not establish current feature availability. `policy-lock.yaml` is a separate artifact, not another block to paste into `bitrouter.yaml`.

### Environment references

| Input | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `-c/--config PATH` | Select an explicit configuration file for commands that accept it. A missing explicit file is an error. |
| `BITROUTER_HOME` | Configuration discovery and runtime home override. A project-local file takes precedence during file discovery. See the [complete discovery order](/docs/routing/configuration#find-the-active-configuration). |
| `${NAME}` inside YAML | Substitute the named environment variable; an undefined variable is a configuration load error. |
| `${NAME:-fallback}` inside YAML | Use the fallback when the variable is unavailable. Substitution in YAML comments is ignored. |
| `RUST_LOG` | Overrides `server.log_level`. The log filter is resolved at process startup. |
| A field named `token_env` | Names the variable containing a dedicated credential; enter the variable's name in YAML, not the token itself. Consult that field's description. |

Provider-specific automatic credential discovery is covered by [BYOK & Subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions#built-in-providers-with-your-own-key). Provider credentials, a client's BitRouter virtual key, and a dedicated control/task API token serve different authentication hops. A YAML `${NAME}` reference can use a variable name you choose; it does not itself register a new automatic provider environment variable.

These file-loading conventions are source-checked against the pinned [configuration loader](https://github.com/bitrouter/bitrouter/blob/54c822a34d4dbfd75d484ca35e108b497048efef/crates/bitrouter-sdk/src/config/mod.rs) and [application paths](https://github.com/bitrouter/bitrouter/blob/54c822a34d4dbfd75d484ca35e108b497048efef/apps/bitrouter/src/paths.rs).

### Reload and restart

The schema does not encode hot-reload support. The pinned [reload implementation](https://github.com/bitrouter/bitrouter/blob/54c822a34d4dbfd75d484ca35e108b497048efef/apps/bitrouter/src/reload.rs) classifies changes against the daemon's startup configuration and live consumers.

| Change | Activation boundary |
| --- | --- |
| Listener, control socket, log filter, authentication mode, or known-pricing admission under `server` | Restart required. |
| Named `routers`, compiled `checkers`, `agents`, MCP connections/aggregation, or plugin configuration | Restart required in this source snapshot. |
| Database URL, native decision backend, recording/retention settings, or continuation retention | Restart required. |
| Provider routing and credentials | Some changes reload, but provider adapter membership, pricing, and other startup-owned consumers can require restart. Do not treat the entire `providers` map as hot-reloadable. |
| Any unclassified or unsupported change | Inspect the daemon's result; do not infer successful activation from a saved file or a valid schema. |

Local `bro reload` can forward provider environment values from the invoking shell. SIGHUP cannot carry newly exported shell values; remote-context reload uses server-owned files without forwarding the client's environment. Check the reload result and `bro status` (`config_state` when available) before relying on new settings. Older daemons may not expose this evidence. See [apply and review changes](/docs/routing/configuration#apply-and-review-changes) for the workflow.

### Top-level fields

These keys belong directly in `bitrouter.yaml`. Unknown top-level keys are rejected.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `acp_recording` | [Acp Recording Config](#acp-recording-config) | No | `{"enabled":false}` |
| `agent_api` | [Agent Api Config](#agent-api-config) | No | Not declared |
| `agents` | Map of `string` → [Acp Agent Config](#acp-agent-config) | No | `{}` |
| `chat` | [Chat Config](#chat-config) | No | Not declared |
| `checkers` | Map of `string` → [Checker Config](#checker-config) | No | `{}` |
| `continuation` | [Continuation Config](#continuation-config) | No | `{"prune_batch_size":1000,"retention_days":30}` |
| `control` | [Control Config](#control-config) | No | Not declared |
| `database` | [Database Config](#database-config) | No | Not declared |
| `decision_model` | [Decision Model Config](#decision-model-config) or `null` | No | `null` |
| `eval` | [Eval Config](#eval-config) | No | `{"authorities":{}}` |
| `inherit_defaults` | `boolean` | No | `true` |
| `mcp` | [Mcp Config](#mcp-config) | No | Not declared |
| `mcp_servers` | Map of `string` → [Mcp Server Config](#mcp-server-config) | No | `{}` |
| `models` | Map of `string` → [Virtual Model](#virtual-model) | No | Not declared |
| `plugins` | Map of `string` → Any JSON value | No | `{}` |
| `policy` | [Policy Config](#policy-config) | No | `{"mode":"frozen","path":null}` |
| `presets` | Map of `string` → [Preset Config](#preset-config) | No | Not declared |
| `providers` | Map of `string` → [Provider Config](#provider-config) | No | Not declared |
| `registry` | [Registry Config](#registry-config) | No | Not declared |
| `routers` | Map of `string` → [Router Config](#router-config) | No | `{}` |
| `server` | [Server Config](#server-config) | No | Not declared |
| `server_tools` | [Server Tools Config](#server-tools-config) | No | Not declared |
| `trajectory` | [Trajectory Config](#trajectory-config) | No | `{"enabled":false,"outbox_batch_size":100,"retention_days":30}` |
| `upstream` | [Upstream Config](#upstream-config) | No | Not declared |
| `variants` | Map of `string` → [Variant Config](#variant-config) | No | Not declared |

- `acp_recording` — Opt-in local storage of observable ACP conversation content.
- `agent_api` — Opt-in privileged BRO coding task API, separate from inference and control.
- `agents` — Upstream ACP agents, keyed by agent id. Surfaced by the `bro agents` CLI (list / check / install). Empty by default.
- `chat` — The interactive session's own configuration.
- `checkers` — Compiled request-check extensions, keyed by the ids referenced from named routers.
- `continuation` — Durable provider continuation mapping lifecycle.
- `control` — Opt-in, read-only operator control API settings.
- `database` — Database connection settings.
- `decision_model` — Typed decision backend for native context routing. Absent means the conservative compiler runs without remote semantic judgments.
- `eval` — Generic evaluation exchange authorities and admission scopes.
- `inherit_defaults` — Whether providers inherit workspace defaults.
- `mcp` — Top-level MCP gateway settings (aggregation, caching). All fields default — `mcp:` is optional in `bitrouter.yaml`.
- `mcp_servers` — Upstream MCP servers, keyed by server id. The id is what appears in `POST /mcp/{id}` and what the `mcp` pipeline's routing table looks up. Empty by default — when empty, the binary does not mount the MCP route.
- `models` — Explicit virtual-model definitions (Strategy 2.2). Optional — when absent, bare model names fall through to Strategy 3 auto-cascade.
- `plugins` — Plugin config, keyed by plugin / bundle id.
- `policy` — Adaptive model-policy settings. A file-backed config resolves the optional path relative to its own directory; when omitted the app looks for `policy-lock.yaml` next to `bitrouter.yaml`. The SDK only carries this declaration -- loading and evolving policy locks belongs to the BitRouter app layer.
- `presets` — `@preset` definitions.
- `providers` — Upstream providers, keyed by provider id.
- `registry` — Public registry integration: whether to fetch + merge the registry's BYOK providers, where to fetch it from, and the provider-class priority ladder used to order the auto-cascade.
- `routers` — Named request routers, addressed as `bitrouter/<id>`.
- `server` — HTTP server settings.
- `server_tools` — Server-side tool loop: MCP server ids whose tools BitRouter injects into LLM requests and executes itself. Empty by default — the pipeline stays single-shot.
- `trajectory` — Durable trajectory progress-control and local operations settings.
- `upstream` — Outbound / upstream HTTP settings (the client that calls providers).
- `variants` — `:variant` definitions.

### Server and connections

#### Server Config

HTTP server settings.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `control_socket` | `string` | No | `"./bitrouter.sock"` |
| `listen` | `string` | No | `"0.0.0.0:4356"` |
| `log_level` | `string` | No | `"info"` |
| `require_known_pricing` | `boolean` | No | `false` |
| `skip_auth` | `boolean` | No | `false` |

- `control_socket` — Unix control socket path.
- `listen` — `host:port` to listen on.
- `log_level` — Log filter for the daemon, in `tracing-subscriber` `EnvFilter` syntax — a bare level (`debug`) or a per-target list (`info,bitrouter=debug`). `RUST_LOG` overrides this when set, following the Rust convention. The filter is resolved once at startup, so changing it needs a restart — `bro reload` will not pick it up. Applies to `bro serve` (and therefore `start`); other subcommands install their subscriber before any config is read and honour `RUST_LOG` only.
- `require_known_pricing` — Deny dispatch when any routed tariff cannot guarantee complete known-price coverage. Decisions caching remains unverified and fails this admission.
- `skip_auth` — SDK-level flag: when `true`, credential-less requests are admitted with a synthesised local caller. Code default is **`false`** — only the config file produced by `bro init` writes `true`.

#### Upstream Config

Outbound / upstream HTTP settings — the client BitRouter uses to call providers. Distinct from `ServerConfig`, which is the inbound listen socket. Currently just `timeouts`; grouped under `upstream:` so future outbound knobs have a home.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `fallback_backoff_ms` | Array of `integer` (`format`: `uint64`; `minimum`: `0`) | No | `[]` |
| `timeouts` | [Timeout Config](#timeout-config) | No | Not declared |

- `fallback_backoff_ms` — Optional delay schedule before advancing through a retryable fallback chain, in milliseconds. The first value applies before the second candidate, the second before the third, and the last value repeats when the chain is longer than the schedule. Empty (the default) preserves immediate fallback.
- `timeouts` — Global upstream timeout defaults. A provider may override any field under `providers.<id>.timeouts:`.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `url` | `string` | No | `"sqlite://./bitrouter.db"` |

- `url` — Connection URL (e.g. `sqlite://./bitrouter.db`).

#### Timeout Config

Upstream HTTP timeout knobs, in seconds. Every field is optional; an unset field inherits the level above — a provider override inherits the resolved global value, and an unset global inherits the built-in default (`HttpTimeouts::default`). `total_secs` is opt-in at every level: unset ⇒ no overall wall-clock cap (the right default for long agentic streams). Used both as the top-level `upstream.timeouts` block and as the per-provider `providers.<id>.timeouts` override; timeouts are **not** inherited via a provider's `derives:` chain.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `connect_secs` | `integer` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `pool_idle_secs` | `integer` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `read_secs` | `integer` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `tcp_keepalive_secs` | `integer` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `total_secs` | `integer` or `null` | No | `null` |

- `connect_secs` — TCP connect timeout, seconds. `format`: `uint64`; `minimum`: `0`
- `pool_idle_secs` — Idle pooled-connection eviction, seconds. `format`: `uint64`; `minimum`: `0`
- `read_secs` — Idle (per-read) timeout, seconds — fires when the upstream sends no bytes for this long, including mid-stream. The effective stream-idle guard. `format`: `uint64`; `minimum`: `0`
- `tcp_keepalive_secs` — TCP keepalive probe interval, seconds. `format`: `uint64`; `minimum`: `0`
- `total_secs` — Overall wall-clock cap for the entire request/stream, seconds. Opt-in: unset ⇒ no cap. Setting it bounds total stream duration, so keep it generous for reasoning / agentic providers. `format`: `uint64`; `minimum`: `0`

#### Provider Config

One upstream provider entry — registry-style. `Debug` redacts `api_key` (v0 audit S9) so a future `tracing::error!(?config, …)` can't dump the platform credential straight into structured logs.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `account_strategy` | [Account Strategy](#account-strategy) | No | Not declared |
| `accounts` | Array of [Provider Account](#provider-account) | No | Not declared |
| `active` | `boolean` | No | `true` |
| `api_base` | `string` | No | `""` |
| `api_key` | `string` | No | `""` |
| `api_protocol` | [Pattern Map for Protocol List](#pattern-map-for-protocol-list) | No | Not declared |
| `auto_discover` | `boolean` | No | `false` |
| `class` | [Provider Class](#provider-class) or `null` | No | Not declared |
| `derives` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `headers` | Map of `string` → [Provider Header Config](#provider-header-config) | No | Not declared |
| `models` | Array of [Provider Model](#provider-model) | No | Not declared |
| `priority` | `integer` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `protocol_endpoints` | Map of `string` → `string` | No | `{}` |
| `rate_limits` | [Pattern Map for Rate Limit](#pattern-map-for-rate-limit) | No | Not declared |
| `tags` | Array of `string` | No | `[]` |
| `timeouts` | [Timeout Config](#timeout-config) | No | Not declared |

- `account_strategy` — How the per-account targets are ordered when `accounts` is set.
- `accounts` — Multiple credentials for this one provider — e.g. two subscriptions to the same upstream. When non-empty, the routing table expands the provider into one routing target per account; `account_strategy` decides their order. Empty = a single-credential provider keyed off the top-level `api_key` (the common case).
- `active` — Whether this provider is active / routable.
- `api_base` — Upstream API base URL.
- `api_key` — Upstream API key (often a `${VAR}` reference).
- `api_protocol` — Glob-prefix `api_protocol` pattern list — each pattern maps to an ordered set of supported wire protocols (the head is the preferred default). Precedence: per-model override > longest matching pattern > host-inferred default. A bare protocol string still parses to a one-element set, so single-protocol providers are unchanged.
- `auto_discover` — When `true` and `models` is empty, discover models from the provider's `/models` endpoint at startup and on reload.
- `class` — Routing-preference class. Set by the public registry merge (or directly in config), then mapped to a numeric rank via `RegistryConfig::provider_priority`. `None` ⇒ unclassed: the provider sorts after every classed one in the auto-cascade (Strategy 3). Plain configs leave this `None`, preserving the alphabetical default order.
- `derives` — Inherit defaults from another provider in this config (acceptance F20 / v0 `derives`). The named provider's `headers`, `api_protocol`, `rate_limits`, `models`, `tags` and `auto_discover` flow into *this* provider's empty fields; explicit fields here win. Resolved by `resolve_derivations` after the config is parsed.
- `headers` — Additional headers applied to every inference request for this provider. A string is shorthand for a static default. The expanded form can opt into forwarding the same inbound header, which overrides the default for that request.
- `models` — Declared model entries. Empty + `auto_discover` triggers discovery.
- `priority` — Explicit routing priority (lower = preferred). When set it overrides the class-derived rank, so an operator can pin one provider ahead of others regardless of class. `None` ⇒ derive the rank from `class`. `format`: `int32`
- `protocol_endpoints` — Optional per-protocol base-URL override, keyed by protocol name (`ApiProtocol::as_str`). When one provider serves different protocols at different paths under a single host — e.g. OpenAI-style under `BASE/v1` and Anthropic Messages under `BASE/anthropic` — give each protocol's base here; protocol-native routing copies the chosen protocol's base onto the routing target. Protocols absent here use `api_base`.
- `rate_limits` — Glob-prefix `rate_limits` pattern list, keyed per matched pattern.
- `tags` — Free-form tags, used by `RoutingPrefs.require_tags` filtering.
- `timeouts` — Per-provider upstream timeout overrides. Each set field layers over the resolved global `UpstreamConfig::timeouts`; unset fields inherit it. Not inherited via `derives`.

#### Account Strategy

How a multi-account provider's per-account targets are ordered.

Exactly one of the following shapes:

**`Alternative 1`**

Accounts in declared order — the first is primary; routing drops to the next on a retryable failure (5xx / 429 / timeout) or a payment / credit-exhaustion error. The default.

Accepted value: `"failover"`.

**`Alternative 2`**

Accounts ordered with a process-random rotation so the primary (and therefore the load) spreads evenly across accounts. The remaining accounts still act as failover targets for that request.

Accepted value: `"balance"`.

#### Virtual Model Strategy

How a `VirtualModel`'s endpoints are ordered into its fallback chain (Strategy 2). Mirrors the typed-enum + serde pattern of `AccountStrategy`. Both strategies build a chain that `execute_with_fallback` walks: a retryable failure (5xx / 408 / 429 / timeout / credit-exhaustion) always advances to the next endpoint — that failover-on-error behaviour is a property of *any* chain and is shared by both. They differ only in the **order** the endpoints take in that chain.

Exactly one of the following shapes:

**`Alternative 1`**

Endpoints are tried in **declared YAML order** — the first is the preferred endpoint, the rest are failover targets reached only when a preceding one fails with a retryable error. Routing preferences (`sort` / `only` / `ignore`) do **not** reorder or filter the chain: the operator's declared priority is authoritative. This is the default and matches the historical (pre-typed-`strategy`) behaviour.

Accepted value: `"priority"`.

**`Alternative 2`**

Endpoints are treated as an unordered candidate set and **re-ordered by the request's `SortOrder`** (the same cascade ordering Strategy-3 auto-cascade applies to providers), and filtered by `only` / `ignore` / `require_tags`. Use this when the endpoints are interchangeable and you want cost/latency-aware (or, today, alphabetical) selection rather than a fixed priority order. `Latency` / `Cost` have no metrics source yet, so they currently fall back to alphabetical-by-provider — the same honest limitation Strategy-3 documents.

Accepted value: `"cascade"`.

#### Capability

An optional inference feature a request may require and a provider may advertise. Capabilities are API-agnostic: the same capability maps to a different wire parameter in each protocol (structured outputs is Chat Completions' `response_format`, Messages' `output_config.format`, Generate Content's `responseSchema`, Responses' `text.format`). The serde representation (e.g. `structured_outputs`) is the stable token used to match a request's needs against a provider's advertised capabilities. A capability-aware `RoutingTable` can read the set a request requires (`Prompt::required_capabilities`) and restrict the chain to providers advertising all of them.

Exactly one of the following shapes:

**`Alternative 1`**

JSON-Schema-constrained output — `ResponseFormat::JsonSchema`.

Accepted value: `"structured_outputs"`.

**`Alternative 2`**

Tool / function calling — the request supplies a non-empty tool list.

Accepted value: `"tools"`.

**`Alternative 3`**

Extended reasoning / thinking — the request sets a reasoning-effort hint.

Accepted value: `"reasoning"`.

**`Alternative 4`**

Provider-side web search / browsing.

Accepted value: `"web_search"`.

**`Alternative 5`**

Token log-probabilities in the response.

Accepted value: `"logprobs"`.

**`Alternative 6`**

Image input (vision) — a message carries an `image/*` file part.

Accepted value: `"image_input"`.

**`Alternative 7`**

Audio input — a message carries an `audio/*` file part.

Accepted value: `"audio_input"`.

| `max_entries_per_server` | `integer` | No | `64` |
| `prompts_list_ttl_secs` | `integer` | No | `300` |
| `resources_list_ttl_secs` | `integer` | No | `60` |
| `resources_templates_list_ttl_secs` | `integer` | No | `300` |
| `tools_list_ttl_secs` | `integer` | No | `60` |

- `enabled` — When `false`, the cache layer is not installed.
- `max_entries_per_server` — LRU safety bound — max entries per server. `format`: `uint`; `minimum`: `0`
- `prompts_list_ttl_secs` — TTL for `prompts/list`. `0` disables for this method. `format`: `uint64`; `minimum`: `0`
- `resources_list_ttl_secs` — TTL for `resources/list`. `0` disables for this method. `format`: `uint64`; `minimum`: `0`
- `resources_templates_list_ttl_secs` — TTL for `resources/templates/list`. `0` disables for this method. `format`: `uint64`; `minimum`: `0`
- `tools_list_ttl_secs` — TTL for `tools/list`. `0` disables for this method. `format`: `uint64`; `minimum`: `0`

#### Mcp Upstream Protocol

`mcp.upstream_protocol` — the startup lifecycle and protocol version the gateway uses when dialing upstream MCP servers. `auto` (the default) starts with modern `server/discover` and uses rmcp's classified legacy fallback. `latest` forces the legacy `initialize` path; `2026-07-28` is the explicit spelling of the modern preference.

Exactly one of the following shapes:

**`Alternative 1`**

Prefer `server/discover` and `2026-07-28`, falling back through rmcp's compatibility path when the upstream identifies itself as legacy.

Accepted value: `"auto"`.

**`Alternative 2`**

Use the legacy `initialize` lifecycle with the latest version the MCP SDK treats as current — today `2025-11-25`.

Accepted value: `"latest"`.

**`Alternative 3`**

Use `server/discover` and the modern `2026-07-28` lifecycle. rmcp falls back after its discovery timeout or a correlated JSON-RPC error it classifies as legacy; transport failures, malformed or uncorrelated responses, and modern rejection codes fail the connection. Opting in also lets upstreams answer `tools/call` with MRTR `input_required` or a Tasks `task` handle; neither is a shape this gateway can carry, so both surface as explicit errors (see `docs/MCP_2026_07_28_SPEC.md` D1).

Accepted value: `"2026-07-28"`.

#### Mcp Transport

How to dial one upstream MCP server. Serde tag is `type: "http" | "stdio"` to match the wire shape used in `bitrouter.yaml`.

Exactly one of the following shapes:

**`type: "http"`**

Streamable HTTP transport — `POST <url>` JSON-RPC with optional SSE responses.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `headers` | Map of `string` → `string` | No | `{}` |
| `type` | `"http"` | Yes | Not declared |
| `url` | `string` | Yes | Not declared |

- `headers` — Static headers added to every request (e.g. `Authorization`).
- `url` — The MCP endpoint URL (e.g. `https://mcp.example.com/v1/mcp`).

**`type: "stdio"`**

Stdio transport — spawn `command` with `args` and exchange JSON-RPC over the child's stdin/stdout.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `args` | Array of `string` | No | `[]` |
| `command` | `string` | Yes | Not declared |
| `env` | Map of `string` → `string` | No | `{}` |
| `type` | `"stdio"` | Yes | Not declared |

- `args` — Arguments to pass to the child.
- `command` — The program to spawn (resolved via `$PATH`).
- `env` — Extra environment variables for the child. Inherited env is kept.

#### Fusion Settings

The `server_tools.fusion` config section. Its presence enables the Fusion server tool and the `bitrouter/fusion` model alias; its fields supply the alias defaults (the panel/judge a bare `bitrouter/fusion` request expands to). An explicit `bitrouter:fusion` declaration on a request overrides these.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `alias` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `judge` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `outer_model` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `panel` | Array of `string` | No | `[]` |
| `synthesizer` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `web_tools` | Array of Any JSON value | No | `[]` |

- `alias` — Alias slug (defaults to `bitrouter/fusion`). Custom aliases cannot use `@preset`, `bitrouter:`, or the reserved `bitrouter/` namespace.
- `judge` — Default judge model (defaults to the first panel model).
- `outer_model` — The model the alias resolves to (defaults to the judge, then the first panel model).
- `panel` — Default panel models the alias expands to.
- `synthesizer` — Optional dedicated synthesizer model.
- `web_tools` — Provider web tools forwarded to every panel member, in provider-namespaced declaration form (e.g. `{type: "<provider>:<tool>"}`).

#### Web Fetch Settings

The `server_tools.web_fetch` section. Its presence enables the `bitrouter:web_fetch` server tool (advertised only when a request declares it). An empty `backends` list leaves the tool effectively off.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `backends` | Array of [Web Fetch Backend Config](#web-fetch-backend-config) | No | Not declared |
| `max_content_tokens` | `integer` or `null` | No | `null` |

- `backends` — Extraction backends in preference/failover order; the first that resolves a key is the default.
- `max_content_tokens` — Default cap on returned content per fetch, in tokens (caller may lower it). Defaults to `DEFAULT_MAX_CONTENT_TOKENS`. `format`: `uint32`; `minimum`: `0`

#### Web Search Settings

The `server_tools.web_search` section. Its presence enables the `bitrouter:web_search` server tool (advertised only when a request declares it). An empty `backends` list leaves the tool effectively off.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `backends` | Array of [Web Search Backend Config](#web-search-backend-config) | No | Not declared |
| `max_results` | `integer` or `null` | No | `null` |

- `backends` — Search backends in preference/failover order; the first that resolves a key is the default.
- `max_results` — Default maximum results per call (caller may lower it). Defaults to `DEFAULT_MAX_RESULTS`. `format`: `uint32`; `minimum`: `0`

#### Web Fetch Backend Config

One configured extraction backend. The `kind` tag selects the engine; the BYOK key resolves from `api_key` (supports `${VAR}` substitution) or, when omitted, the engine's conventional environment variable.

Exactly one of the following shapes:

**`kind: "exa"`**

exa.ai `/contents` — key `api_key` or `EXA_API_KEY`.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `api_base` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `api_key` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `kind` | `"exa"` | Yes | Not declared |

- `api_base` — Endpoint override (else the engine default).
- `api_key` — Explicit API key (else `EXA_API_KEY`).

**`kind: "firecrawl"`**

firecrawl.dev `/v2/scrape` — key `api_key` or `FIRECRAWL_API_KEY`.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `api_base` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `api_key` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `kind` | `"firecrawl"` | Yes | Not declared |

- `api_base` — Endpoint override (else the engine default).
- `api_key` — Explicit API key (else `FIRECRAWL_API_KEY`).

**`kind: "tavily"`**

tavily.com `/extract` — key `api_key` or `TAVILY_API_KEY`.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `api_base` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `api_key` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `kind` | `"tavily"` | Yes | Not declared |

- `api_base` — Endpoint override (else the engine default).
- `api_key` — Explicit API key (else `TAVILY_API_KEY`).

#### Web Search Backend Config

One configured search backend. The `kind` tag selects the engine; the BYOK key resolves from `api_key` (supports `${VAR}` substitution) or, when omitted, the engine's conventional environment variable.

Exactly one of the following shapes:

**`kind: "parallel"`**

parallel.ai — key `api_key` or `PARALLEL_API_KEY`.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `api_base` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `api_key` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `kind` | `"parallel"` | Yes | Not declared |

- `api_base` — Endpoint override (else the engine default).
- `api_key` — Explicit API key (else `PARALLEL_API_KEY`).

**`kind: "exa"`**

exa.ai — key `api_key` or `EXA_API_KEY`.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `api_base` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `api_key` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `kind` | `"exa"` | Yes | Not declared |

- `api_base` — Endpoint override (else the engine default).
- `api_key` — Explicit API key (else `EXA_API_KEY`).

**`kind: "firecrawl"`**

firecrawl.dev — key `api_key` or `FIRECRAWL_API_KEY`.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `api_base` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `api_key` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `kind` | `"firecrawl"` | Yes | Not declared |

- `api_base` — Endpoint override (else the engine default).
- `api_key` — Explicit API key (else `FIRECRAWL_API_KEY`).

**`kind: "tavily"`**

tavily.com — key `api_key` or `TAVILY_API_KEY`.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `api_base` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `api_key` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `kind` | `"tavily"` | Yes | Not declared |

- `api_base` — Endpoint override (else the engine default).
- `api_key` — Explicit API key (else `TAVILY_API_KEY`).

**`kind: "native"`**

A web-search-capable model whose *native* search tool is forwarded, made available to every model routed through BitRouter.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `kind` | `"native"` | Yes | Not declared |
| `model` | `string` | Yes | Not declared |
| `name` | `string` or `null` | No | `null` |
| `tool` | `any` | Yes | Not declared |

- `model` — The search-capable model serving the call.
- `name` — Backend id the caller pins (e.g. `"native"`); defaults to `"native"`.
- `tool` — The provider-defined native search tool, e.g. `{ "type": "anthropic:web_search_20250305" }`.

### Retention and recording

#### Trajectory Config

Durable trajectory progress-control settings.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `boolean` | No | `false` |
| `outbox_batch_size` | `integer` | No | `100` |
| `retention_days` | `integer` | No | `30` |

- `enabled` — Explicit opt-in for durable trajectory routing and settlement.
- `outbox_batch_size` — Maximum durable outbox rows attempted in one publication batch. `format`: `uint`; `minimum`: `0`
- `retention_days` — Age boundary used by startup retention, in whole days. `format`: `uint32`; `minimum`: `0`

#### Acp Recording Config

Local ACP conversation content recording, independent of routing evidence.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `boolean` | No | `false` |

- `enabled` — Store observable session messages and tool results until explicitly deleted. No content is recorded or sent to an evaluator by default.

#### Continuation Config

Always-active durable provider continuation lifecycle settings.

| Field | Type | Required | Schema default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `prune_batch_size` | `integer` | No | `1000` |
| `retention_days` | `integer` | No | `30` |

- `prune_batch_size` — Maximum expired rows removed by one prune operation. `format`: `uint`; `minimum`: `0`
- `retention_days` — Days before a continuation becomes unusable. `format`: `uint32`; `minimum`: `0`

content/docs/(guide)/routing/context-rou.content:
---
title: Context Routing
description: Adjust what the next model call sees while preserving the evidence collected during the same task.
---

A task can collect more history than its next step needs: file reads, tool results, failed attempts, and earlier conclusions. BitRouter's native managed runtime builds a **context view** for the next model call from that retained evidence. As the task progresses, the view can change while the original evidence remains available. This selects what the next call sees; [Strategies](/docs/routing/strategies) explains model and provider selection.

<Callout type="info">
This page describes context views in the native managed runtime. Availability depends on the runtime and build you use. Routing an external harness's model traffic through BitRouter does not give BitRouter control of that harness's history or compaction.
</Callout>

## One task, different views

The task and its acceptance criteria stay in place. What changes is the historical material supplied to the next model call.

For example, an agent fixing an authentication bug might first inspect several modules, then focus on a failing test. The next view can retain the relevant source and failure output, use an available summary for an earlier investigation, and leave unrelated historical output out of that call. If the agent later needs an omitted detail, it can search the retained evidence and recall its original source.

| Stage | Evidence available to the task | Context for the next call |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Investigate | File reads, searches, and initial findings | Required instructions, recent work, and relevant source material |
| Fix | Investigation history plus a failing test | Required and recent material, with eligible older evidence kept, summarized, extracted, or omitted |
| Verify | Earlier investigation, edits, and new test output | Recent verification evidence plus any older source explicitly recalled |

This example illustrates how a view can evolve; a particular reduction is subject to the evidence's eligibility and the selection decision.

## How a view is built

1. **Retain the evidence.** Historical messages are grouped into source blocks. Tool calls and their results stay together, and each block retains its source identity.
2. **Protect required material.** Instructions, user messages, provider continuity data, recent groups, and explicitly recalled sources are retained as required by the runtime's rules.
3. **Assess eligible history.** A bounded set of older, optional blocks is assessed against the current task, acceptance criteria, and instructions. Blocks outside that candidate set remain in full.
4. **Compile the next input.** BitRouter applies eligible selections, validates the resulting history, and checks its hard size limit before execution.

The selection can use these representations:

| Representation | What the model receives | What remains stored |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Full | The complete source group | The original group |
| Extract | Exact selected spans, labeled as historical evidence | The original group and its source references |
| Summary | An available task-specific summary, labeled as derived evidence | The original group and the summary's source references |
| Omitted | No content from that optional block in this call | The original group, available for search and recall |

Extracts and summaries are eligible only when a compatible representation already exists and the context policy detects size pressure. Selecting a smaller view does not itself generate a summary of every old block.

## Search and recall

The native runtime provides evidence operations to the model when context views are enabled:

| Operation | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `context_search` | Find retained evidence, including material omitted from the current view |
| `context_recall` | Pin complete source groups into the next task view |
| `context_publish` | Publish a task-specific summary of an optional source group the agent has read |
| `context_extract` | Publish exact text spans as a smaller representation of an optional source group |

These operations work within the task's admitted evidence. Recalling historical file contents does not establish that the workspace is still in that state; the agent should read current files again before relying on them for an edit.

## When reduction is unsafe

An uncertain or missing selection keeps the source in full. Required blocks cannot be omitted, and a summary or extract cannot replace a source when its compatibility checks fail. Provider continuity data and complete tool exchanges must preserve a valid model history.

If the required and conservatively retained material still exceeds the hard prompt limit, BitRouter rejects that execution plan. It does not silently discard required evidence to make the call fit.

A smaller input can reduce input-token use, but assessment and summary generation also consume resources. Savings depend on the selected model, the retained material, and the work needed to build the view.

## Context selection and model routing

Context selection determines **what the next call sees**. Model routing determines **which model serves it**. [Virtual Models](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models) explains how callers name model endpoints; changing the context does not require changing that name.

The task continues with its retained evidence as the view changes. This does not migrate an external agent's session or switch the CLI's named remote target. The separate [`bro context` commands](/docs/usage/cli#bro-context) select remote administration targets.

<Cards>
  <Card title="Strategies" href="/docs/routing/strategies" description="Understand policy-bound model selection separately from context views." />
  <Card title="Virtual Models" href="/docs/models-routing/virtual-models" description="Give model endpoints a reusable name." />
</Cards>

content/docs/(guide)/routing/routing-tra.content:
---
title: Routing Traces
description: Trace routing decisions across your workflow, from the requested model to the serving route and its recorded outcome.
---

See which models served each step of a workflow, how routes changed, and what those choices cost. Routing Traces connects the router's decisions with the requests and upstream attempts that actually ran.

## Follow the workflow trajectory

An agent may inspect files, make changes, call tools, and verify a result across many model requests. Inspect the routing evidence in that execution order, rather than treating each model call as an unrelated event.

For each observable step, compare:

| Question | Evidence to inspect |
| --- | --- |
| What did the caller request? | The model selector and the request's workflow or trace association, when available |
| What did the router select? | The resolved model, provider, and recorded decision evidence |
| What actually executed? | The upstream attempts, retry or fallback transitions, and final serving route |
| What did that choice consume? | Recorded token usage, cost, latency, and execution status |
| What changed between steps? | Model or provider changes and policy identity or context-selection evidence, where recorded |

A selected route and the final serving route can differ after a fallback. Keep the decision, attempted executions, and settled result distinct.

## Start with a request

For a local deployment, inspect recent settled requests:

```bash
bro requests --limit 25
```

[Request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts) distinguish the requested selector from the resolved model and serving provider. Match a request to your workflow using the available request identifiers and recorded correlation evidence. Timestamp proximity alone does not establish that two requests belong to the same workflow.

Cloud Activity and `bro cloud requests --limit 25` provide Cloud request records. Receipts summarize settled requests; they are not a complete workflow timeline.

## Inspect routing and upstream attempts

For more detail, configure [OpenTelemetry export](/docs/self-hosting#opentelemetry) and inspect the trace in your OTLP backend. BitRouter exports ingress and routing spans, upstream attempt spans, and settlement metadata. Retry and fallback attempts remain separate hops.

Use the parent-child span relationships and propagated trace context to place router activity alongside the caller's instrumented workflow. Expand a request to compare its routing activity with each attempted model execution, then return to the surrounding workflow to see how later steps proceeded.

Recorded rule matches, candidate constraints, policy identity, or decision evidence can explain a choice when the runtime emits them. An absent explanation is missing evidence; it is not permission to infer a model's private reasoning or an unrecorded decision.

## Understand coverage

<Callout type="info">
Workflow coverage depends on the runtime, correlation evidence, instrumentation, and sampling. Routing an external harness through BitRouter exposes the model requests it sends to the router; it does not automatically expose every tool action, private session event, or internal context change in that harness.
</Callout>

Check the scope of the evidence before drawing conclusions:

- **Request coverage:** which model requests reached this BitRouter instance and were retained or exported?
- **Workflow correlation:** which requests have an established shared workflow or trace association?
- **Attempt coverage:** which upstream attempts and outcomes were recorded?
- **Agent coverage:** which tool and agent events were emitted by the host itself?

Keep unresolved associations and gaps visible. A successful request does not prove task success, and a lower request cost does not prove that the workflow improved.

## Policy evidence and evaluations

<a id="policy-artifacts-and-audit-boundaries" />
<a id="let-evidence-improve-the-policy" />
<a id="review-and-publish-a-change" />
<a id="evaluations" />
<a id="two-evidence-paths" />
<a id="evidence-lifecycle" />
<a id="1-define-and-seal-a-subject" />
<a id="2-evaluate-outside-the-router" />
<a id="3-submit-the-result" />
<a id="4-freeze-a-snapshot" />
<a id="5-consume-the-evidence-explicitly" />
<a id="reproducibility-boundary" />
<a id="what-evaluation-does-not-establish" />
<a id="inspect-the-active-policy" />

[Workload Optimization](/docs/routing/workload-optimization) introduces learning from recurring work. Its [existing policy tools](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#existing-policy-tools) document policy artifacts, evaluation evidence, and reviewed publication. A trace can supply observations for evaluation; collecting it does not automatically approve a policy change.

For sections moved from Auditable Policies, continue to [policy artifacts](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#policy-artifacts-and-audit-boundaries), [policy evidence](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#let-evidence-improve-the-policy), [evaluations](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#evaluations), or [review and publication](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#review-and-publish-a-change).

<Cards>
  <Card title="Request receipts" href="/docs/cli/request-receipts" description="Inspect requested selectors, actual serving routes, usage, and status." />
  <Card title="OpenTelemetry" href="/docs/self-hosting#opentelemetry" description="Configure export, content capture, and sampling for your trace backend." />
  <Card title="Workload Optimization" href="/docs/routing/workload-optimization" description="Understand the planned learning loop and the existing evaluation and policy tools." />
</Cards>

content/docs/(guide)/routing/strategies..content:
---
title: Strategies
description: Resolve selectors, constrain eligible providers, and reuse routing rules through presets and named variants.
---

Routing strategies determine **which models and providers are eligible for a call and how their candidates are ordered**. A [virtual model](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models) defines a reusable model endpoint; routing resolves the caller's selector, forms the eligible candidate set, and applies the configured selection behavior. [Context Routing](/docs/routing/context-routing) independently determines what retained evidence the next native model call sees.

## How a call is routed

1. **Resolve the selector.** Resolve a named router, virtual model, legacy preset, or explicit provider/model route.
2. **Apply a bound policy when present.** A policy-bound local router selects a configured tier from the request's routing fingerprint. An unmatched fingerprint uses the conservative default tier.
3. **Resolve eligible endpoints.** Apply the selected route's endpoint rules, capabilities, protocol, credentials, and caller-access requirements.
4. **Execute and inspect.** Retryable upstream failures may advance the eligible chain. A settled receipt records the route that actually served the call.

| Requested selector | Selection behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `bitrouter/auto` | Use the policy bound to the local `auto` router; initialize the binding before use |
| A virtual model such as `coding` | Resolve its configured endpoints using its declared strategy |
| A logical model id such as `openai/gpt-5.4` | Select that model across eligible connected providers |
| `openai:openai/gpt-5.4` | Pin one configured provider and model |

Use [Auto Router](/docs/routing/auto-router) for policy-bound model selection, or configure candidate rules below. [Virtual Models](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models#model-selector-forms) documents selector syntax and resolution order.

## Choose a routing approach


| Approach | Choose it when | Configuration surface |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ordered endpoints | You want a declared primary endpoint and explicit replacements | A virtual model with `strategy: priority` |
| Candidate-based selection | Endpoints are interchangeable and provider preferences should filter or reorder them | A bare logical model or a virtual model with `strategy: cascade`, plus routing preferences |
| Policy-bound selection | Different request fingerprints should use configured strong/economy tiers | A named router bound to `policy-lock.yaml`, such as `bitrouter/auto` |

The available building blocks have different scopes. A named local router supplies model selection and request defaults. Legacy presets remain available for compatibility. The `strategy` field on a virtual model controls its endpoint resolution. A policy binding adds tier selection. Account strategies select credentials within a provider and are described in [Model Fallbacks](/docs/models-routing/model-fallback#account-fallback).

### Ordered endpoints

Define a [virtual model](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models#define-a-virtual-model) with `strategy: priority` and put its endpoints in the order you want them attempted. Change the endpoint list to customize that order. A retryable failure may advance the chain; an unsatisfactory successful answer does not itself trigger fallback.

### Candidate-based selection

Use `strategy: cascade` when endpoint preferences may filter and reorder a virtual model's alternatives. A bare logical model resolves across connected providers declaring that model. Both paths can use the routing preferences below; connected models still need compatible capabilities and protocols.

### Policy-bound selection

Use [Auto Router](/docs/routing/auto-router) when model selection should depend on request fingerprints and configured policy tiers. Calling `bitrouter/auto` without the binding fails visibly; the model name alone does not install a usable policy.

## Inference pool

The **inference pool** is the set of connected models and provider routes a request may consider. Supply can come from your own provider credentials, local or private endpoints, or inference access obtained through BitRouter. Buying or selling inference is optional; routing uses existing access and does not purchase supply.

Connection alone does not make a source eligible for every request. Membership uses the existing provider, router, preset, and variant settings in `bitrouter.yaml`; there is no separate `pool:` block.

Connect sources with [BYOK & Subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions) or [Local Models](/docs/models-routing/local-models).

## Inspect the connected sources

```bash
bro providers list
bro models
bro models --provider openai
bro route openai/gpt-5.4
```

`bro models` shows available model identities. `bro route` previews the candidate chain for a selector without sending an inference request. [Request receipts](/docs/cli/request-receipts) identify the model and provider that actually served a call.

## Candidate eligibility

For a bare model, BitRouter filters active providers by `only`, `ignore`, required tags, request capabilities, and protocol compatibility. It then orders candidates by explicit provider priority or the registry's provider-class priority, followed by provider ID.

A `cascade` virtual model also applies routing preferences to its candidate endpoints. A `priority` virtual model preserves its explicitly declared endpoint chain: preference filters such as `only`, `ignore`, and `require_tags` do not prune that chain. To restrict a priority chain, edit its endpoints. Capability and protocol compatibility still apply.

Configure the filters and release-specific ordering behavior below.

## Configure routing rules


Choose the models and providers first, then configure candidate constraints and endpoint order for the selected approach. This guide covers composing existing settings and policy artifacts; it does not define an arbitrary user-code plugin interface for new selection algorithms.

### Request presets

Define a reusable local router under `routers`. For example,
this fragment selects one logical model and restricts its provider candidates:

```yaml
routers:
  openai_only:
    selection:
      kind: model
      model: openai/gpt-5.4
      routing:
        only: [openai]
```

Configure the `openai` provider separately, then inspect the named router:

```bash
bro config validate -c bitrouter.yaml
bro route bitrouter/openai_only -c bitrouter.yaml
bro claude --model bitrouter/openai_only
```

Change the model or provider list to customize this profile. To choose among
different models by request fingerprint, initialize an [Auto Router policy binding](/docs/routing/auto-router#initialize-a-policy-binding).
[Virtual Models](/docs/models-routing/virtual-models#presets) covers request defaults
and their precedence. Legacy `@name` selectors address presets. On Cloud, use a catalog model ID or an enabled workspace preset addressed as `@<name>`.

### Variants

A named routing variant applies reusable candidate preferences. Define it under `variants:` and apply it with a `:variant` suffix. It modifies routing behavior without creating a model version or another virtual-model definition:

```yaml
variants:
  private:
    routing:
      require_tags: [private]
  primary:
    routing:
      only: [openai]
```

Append a known variant to a logical model or preset, for example `openai/gpt-5.4:primary` or `@fast:primary`. Configure the referenced providers and presets first. The `private` variant requires matching provider tags; its name does not establish a privacy guarantee. Named local routers do not generally accept variant suffixes. `bitrouter/auto` retains its compatibility variants. An unknown suffix remains part of the selector.

Router, legacy preset, and variant `routing` blocks accept `only`, `ignore`, and `require_tags`. These constrain bare-model and cascade selection. They do not prune a `priority` virtual model's authoritative endpoint list: remove disallowed endpoints from that list instead. Filters do not grant access, bypass guardrails, or supply credentials.

### Ordering and release limits

Use provider `priority` for explicit provider order in candidate-based selection, or `strategy: priority` and endpoint order for an explicit virtual-model chain. Presets and variants also accept these sort values:

| Value | alpha.33 behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `alphabetical` | Provider priority, then provider ID |
| `cost` | Accepted, but currently uses the same deterministic fallback order |
| `latency` | Accepted, but currently uses the same deterministic fallback order |

<Callout type="warning">
The self-hosted alpha.33 proxy uses deterministic ordering. Hosted `:cost`, `:latency`, and `:throughput` profiles bias a separate Cloud ranking.
</Callout>

## Capability and protocol constraints

The request can require tool calling, structured outputs, or another model capability. An endpoint that explicitly lacks a required capability cannot become eligible merely because it is included in a virtual model or a preferred provider list.

For custom sources, declare only verified capabilities in [BYOK & Subscriptions](/docs/models-routing/byok-subscriptions#custom-endpoints-and-models). BitRouter normalizes the request, derives its requirements, and renders the selected route in its outbound protocol. A protocol's ability to encode a feature does not establish that a specific model implements it.

[Responses API](/docs/usage/responses-api#structured-outputs-across-protocols) documents response-format fields across supported protocols. Use the subset supported by every endpoint that may receive the request; translation cannot invent fields the destination cannot represent.

## Scope and routing boundaries

- A provider-qualified selector pins one provider; it does not expand into the rest of the pool.
- Subscription sources require an explicit provider-qualified route. Bare model selection does not silently consume a personal subscription.
- A virtual model names configured endpoints; it does not automatically include every connected model.
- Routing filters narrow candidates. They do not grant credentials or caller access.
- [Model Fallbacks](/docs/models-routing/model-fallback) controls replacement after a retryable failure; it does not make an incompatible model eligible.

[Context Routing](/docs/routing/context-routing) selects the evidence supplied to the next native model call. That context view is a separate selection from the model/provider candidate pool.

## Policy-driven selection and evidence

A bound model policy maps request fingerprints to configured tiers. In alpha.33, frozen and adaptive modes both use the lock for request-time routing. Adequacy fields remain inputs for policy compilation. Objective-scored evaluations use explicitly admitted evidence.

[Auto Router](/docs/routing/auto-router#initialize-a-policy-binding) covers initialization. [Workload Optimization](/docs/routing/workload-optimization#existing-policy-tools) covers policy compilation, reviewed publication, and evaluation evidence. Evidence collection does not automatically publish a candidate policy. The policy artifact does not establish a context-loading contract for an external harness.

## Decisions API and policy ownership

[Decisions API](/docs/reference/decisions) evaluates typed questions over supplied evidence. A decision response alone does not create a routing policy, admit evaluation results, or publish a candidate. The routing runtime applies its own policy and execution constraints.

<Cards>

  <Card title="Auto Router" href="/docs/routing/auto-router" description="Initialize bitrouter/auto and inspect a policy-bound request." />
  <Card title="Routing Traces" href="/docs/routing/routing-traces" description="Inspect routing behavior and upstream attempts across a workflow." />

  <Card title="Context Routing" href="/docs/routing/context-routing" description="Select evidence for the next native model call." />
</Cards>

## Auto routing setup

## Policy lifecycle and evidence
